speakeroldname: Hon. E. B. RYCKMAN (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
The hon. member for
North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) yesterday asked me a question, which I said I would answer to-day, in regard to the possibility of reducing the value of the pound sterling for customs purposes from $4.86f to a lower figure. All customs rates for duty were originally fixed upon that value.
I feel that at the present time, in view of the disturbed condition of exchange quotations, it would be unwise for us to consider

any alteration in the present arrangement until it becomes apparent that exchange quotations are more stabilized. Changed circumstances with changed requirements may quickly come.
It might be appropriate at this time, however, without entering into too much detail, to explain to the house the circumstances which prompted the government to establish the present basis.
In September, 1931, the commodity price index wholesale in Great Britain as published in the Bank of England Statistical Summary was 99.2. In that month, as all hon. members are aware, Great Britain suspended payments in gold, and the immediate result was an increase in commodity prices in Great Britain. For October, 1931, the figure was 104.4, and in November, 106.4. Since that time the index figure has moved closer to the 100 mark, and in the month of October, 1932, it stood at 101.1, November 101.1, and in December, the last month for which figures are available, it was 101. Comparing that ' figure, therefore, with the index as in September, 1931, it will be noted that there is actually a slight increase in wholesale prices in Great Britain.
If prompt action had not been taken by our government in September, 1931, to continue to value the pound sterling for customs purposes at |486f, the net result would have beeD that the tariff against Great Britain up to about twenty per cent would have been wiped out, and in some cases indeed the British exporter to Canada would, owing to exchange, be receiving a bonus.
Action could perhaps have been taken by way of special surtax or quota system as has been done by other countries who were faced with unfair competition from countries whose currency had become depreciated, but we adopted the more moderate course of endeavouring to maintain so far as was possible the status quo, with this slight exception that having regard to the fact that there had been an increase in commodity prices in Great Britain variously estimated by experts at the time at anywhere from seven per cent to ten per cent, we decided that although regular duty would be assessed on the basis of $4.86f to the pound sterling, special or exchange dumping duty would only be collected on a basis of $4.40 to the pound sterling, which represents approximately a discount of ten per cent from the par value.
Since that time representations have been made to me both to increase and to lower the

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Manion
figure of $4.40, but everything considered I believe it has been fair and reasonable to all interests affected.
As I stated at the outset, I do not believe this would be an opportune time to make any [DOT]change in this arrangement.
While speaking of matters pertaining to the Department of National Revenue, perhaps the minister would explain the rulings given yesterday by his department and the reasons therefor.

There was only one ruling made by the minister of which the minister had any knowledge. It happens in the ordinary course of business that it is necessary to determine on the spot how an entry should be treated. The result was that our officials were consulted with regard to an entry and, not knowing at what rate the exchange should be computed, they inquired of one of our largest banks as to what they were to do as respects exchange. The answer came that the last rate that was published was $1.18. If they wished to be secured against risk, they would be safe in putting it at $1.25 and making their adjustment afterwards. They adopted the course taken upon the statement of the bank that that was the proper thing to do. Owing to an indisposition I was not in the house yesterday afternoon or evening, but I read the announcements made in the evening papers. I considered the matter, consulted with those who were interested and made up my mind that in view of the- special emergency in the United States and the fact that the par rate is dollar for dollar and no quotations were available, and as some special order had to be given, the fair thing to do would be to set a rate of par for par until we had some different information. With that in view I sought to make it clear that it would be only fair at this time and until the matter was settled, whioh will be no doubt by Friday, that par for par and dollar for dollar should be the prevailing rate.
Having in mind what the minister has just said, I should like to know if it is customary for an official in his department to give a ruling and make an order without the knowledge of the minister?

I do not think that is so. I have explained the circumstances in this case and, frankly, I can imagine some measure of excuse for a collector at a port telephoning
to the bank and asking for its best knowledge upon the matter and acting in accordance with what the bank thought he ought to do.
I think we would do likewise.
No ministerial responsibility.

Hon. R. J. MANION (Minister of Railways and Canals) moved the second reading of Bill No. 37, respecting the Canadian National Railways and to provide for cooperation with the Canadian Pacific Railway system, and for other purposes.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not think it is necessary at this stage of the discussion for me to give any detailed explanation of the bill now before the house. It will be sufficient to say that the bill contains three parts, the first dealing entirely with the Canadian National Railways and the second and third with the two transcontinental railways. The first part deals with the appointment of trustees for the Canadian National Railways, the auditing of its accounts, its annual budget and its annual report to the parliament of Canada; the second part deals with suggested methods of cooperation between the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the third part provides for the setting up of arbitral tribunals for the settlement of disagreements or disputes arising out of the proposed cooperation.
As the house well knows, this bill is based upon the report of the royal commission on transportation, sometimes called the Duff commission. That commission wTas appointed on November 20, 1931, and made its report on September 13, 1932. The commission was appointed not at the request of this or any other government but really upon the proposal of the heads of the two railways. In the first place, it was proposed by Sir Henry Thornton when he appeared before the select standing committee on railways and shipping, which committee reported to the house on July 16, 1931, in the following words:
Your committee desire to call the attention of the house to the proposal made by Sir Henry Thornton at one of the sessions of the
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Manion

committee. He referred to file serious position of the transportation business generally and recommended that a commission be appointed for the purpose of considering the whole question of Canadian transportation. Your committee regard such a recommendation coming from such a source at this time as worthy of the serious consideration of the government.
A moment ago I stated that the appointment of this committee had been proposed by the heads of the two railway companies, and I think the Canadian Pacific Railway can be linked up by a statement made recently by Mr. Beatty before the Canadian Club of Toronto. A pamphlet was circulated, I assume by the Canadian Pacific Railway, entitled, "An Address delivered by E. W. Beatty, Iv.C., LL.D., chairman and president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, before the Canadian Club." This speech was delivered on January 16 last. Mr. Beatty said:
We come now to the events of the last two years. In 1931, during one of the sessions of the special committee of the House of Commons which has annually considered the report and appropriations of the Canadian National Railways, questions were asked which led me to think that the time would be opportune for an inquiry into the whole question of transportation in Canada by an independent tribunal; that much good might result and that at least there would be given much information of value to the public as a whole.
I had for two years prior been very apprehensive as to the railway situation. Our traffic had fallen rapidly, our debts had increased and the deficits of the national lines were great. So I conferred with the former president of the national railways and suggested to him that during the course of his examination by the committee he might advise such an investigation as I had in mind. He readily agreed and made such a recommendation. It was unanimously adopted by the committee and later was unanimously approved by the House of Commons. The government acted upon the recommendation of the house, and the so-called Duff commission was dn due course appointed.
I quote this speech of Mr. Beatty's in order to show that the heads of the two railway companies were unanimous in suggesting the appointment of this commission. It will be remembered that when the select committee on railways and shipping made its report to the house, that report included the clause which I read a moment ago. The report of that committee was unanimously adopted by this house and as far as I know it was supported generally by the press and public of this country. The government felt it to be its duty to look around and endeavour to find a commission which would be above party politics and have such outstanding ability that its report would be accepted with a great deal of confidence by the people of this country.
[Mr. Manion.1
A commission was appointed with the Right Honourable Mr. Justice Duff, an outstanding jurist of Canada, as chairman. There were also upon the commission representatives of Great Britain and the United States, it being felt that such representation should be had upon the commission in view of the fact that the bonds and stocks of the Canadian Pacific Railway were held to a large extent in Great Britain, while the bonds of the Canadian National Railway were held to a large extent in the United States. It was felt to be only fair that these shareholders should be represented upon a commission in whom they would have special confidence. Lord Ashfield, a gentleman who had made a reputation in the United States and later on in Great Britain in transportation matters was appointed. Another appointment made was Mr. Loree, the president of the Delaware and Hudson Railway. While not the president of one of the larger railways in the United States, Mr. Loree was looked upon by most people in that country as one of the outstanding authorities upon railway matters. He has succeeded in carrying his own railway through these very trying times in a splendid condition. The other Canadian representatives besides the Right Honourable Mr. Justice Duff were Sir Joseph Flavelle, who was for some time in the years gone by the chairman of the Grand Trunk Canadian board and who is an outstanding business executive of this country; Beaudry Leman, of Quebec, who had recently been president of the Canadian Bankers' Association and who, in addition, was a well known civil engineer- before he went into banking; Doctor Webster, of Shediac, New Brunswick, a gentleman who had made a reputation in his own profession not only in the United States, but in Scotland as well as throughout the world, and who had that gift few doctors have of being such a good businessman that some years ago he was able to retire from his profession and give, from his native town, Shediac, his services to his country in various lines of endeavour. Finally, there was Professor Murray of Saskatchewan university, who, it was felt, would bring to bear upon the matter the western viewpoint as well as the university-economic viewpoint, if I may so describe it. Therefore I say that we appointed what might well be considered a very distinguished and able commission to deal with this problem, and so far as this bill is concerned, it agrees practically in toto with the report made by that commission. There are some differences in matters of very minor detail, but the principles included in the bill

C.N.R -C JP.R. Bill-Mr. Manion
are based entirely on the report of the commission.
Speaking of the report generally, I may say that it was a summing up of the whole transportation situation of Canada. It showed the urgent need of economies if the railways of our country were to get back into a prosperous condition. It pointed out the dangers to the people of Canada if steps were not taken to get the railways back into a proper state of economic operation and management. It advocated very emphatically greater cooperation than had existed in past years between the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways. Finally, it suggested methods whereby its proposals might be put into effect. I think at this moment it might be well for me to quote the warning-I doubt whether it has been quoted in the house before, but it has been quoted a great deal in the press-given by the commission in regard to the situation of the transportation companies in Canada. They said in paragraph 226 of the report:
We feel compelled, as a matter of public duty, to strike a serious note of warning to the people of Canada. Unless the country is prepared to adopt the plan we have proposed, or some other equally effective measures, to secure the efficient and economical working of both railway systems and thereby not only reduce the burden on the federal treasury but improve the financial position of the privately-owned railway, then the only courses that would be left would be either to effect savings in national expenditure in other directions, or to add still further to the burdens under which the industries of the country are suffering by the imposition of yet further taxation. Failing the adoption of one or other of these courses, and there are obvious limits to their application, the very stability of the nation's finances and the financial credit of the Canadian Pacific Railway will be threatened, with serious consequences to the people of Canada and to those who have invested their savings in that railway.
I may just interject at this moment that some members of the government, notably the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and I as Minister of Railways have at various times in the last couple of years been uttering practically the same warning, and so far as I am concerned I have used on nearly every occasion the same examples or some of them which were used by the transportation commission. I am afraid that the only reward I received, at any rate from one section of the press, was the charge that I was showing enmity to the Canadian National by merely giving the facts. But I submit that no word of mine at any time has been more emphatic in regard to the dangers of the situation than this utterance of the transportation commission. In regard to danger of enmity to the Canadian National may I add this: I believe
there is no Canadian, to whatever part of Canada or to whatever party in politics he belongs, who does not realize that we are all deeply and heavily involved from a financial standpoint in the future of the Canadian National Railways, and who does not feel a very sincere responsibility for it, and a very sincere desire for its return to prosperity. In other words, I think it is the wish of hon. members, in whatever portion of the house they may sit, that the Canadian National may be brought back to an economic situation where it may be able to carry on equally well with the other great transportation company of this dominion.
The remedies proposed by the transportation commission were, in brief, as follows: First, they said that there should be no amalgamation of the two railways. I have read over this bill many times and I submit that in it there is nothing that in any way conflicts with that recommendation. Second, they said that the deficits should be voted. In other words, in the future at any rate, whatever may have been the custom in the past, they suggest that we should not put on the railways mortgages consisting of deficits in regard to the payment of interest charges. Third, they suggest the selection of auditors by parliament from a panel presented to the House of Commons. Fourth, they suggest that instead of the seventeen directors now in control of the Canadian National Railways, there should be a board of three trustees, one of whom would be chairman, giving his full time to the work of attending to the financial end of that railway, and the other two close at hand in order to be able to consult with the chairman at all times. Fifth, they suggest, as I have pointed out before, very much greater cooperation and consultation to bring about that cooperation between the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways, and, finally, they provide for the setting up of arbitral tribunals in case there may arise disagreements or disputes in carrying out the proposed cooperations, whether proposed by one railway or by the other.
As one looks around the country, one is struck, and I think all citizens who have thought on the matter at all have been struck by the opportunities of economy from the standpoint of cooperation between the two great railway systems. One has only to walk down Sparks street, two or three blocks from where we are sitting here this afternoon, and past two ticket and telegraph offices on that street within a few doors of each other, occupying very highly priced premises, and within a couple of blocks of the union station, to see a duplication which, to the ordinary

C.N.R ,-C .P.R. Bill-Mr. Manion
man at any rate, is certainly unnecessary. This occurs in many of our cities. The same is true at least to a certain extent in regard to duplication of train services throughout the country, although I may say that at times I have come to the conclusion, particularly since the railways have dealt with the matter in some degree, the duplication of trains is somewhat exaggerated. Let me illustrate that by the trains running between Montreal and Ottawa which are often cited by hon. members as being too numerous, and that certainly seem to be so. The other day I looked into the matter and I found that there were three trains in each direction operated by the Canadian National and six trains in each direction operated by the Canadian Pacific. This sounds like a great and unnecessary number of trains to be operating between these two cities. But it must not be forgotten that, for example, in the case of the Canadian National, one of those trains is a transcontinental and is not primarily operated for service between Montreal and Ottawa. Therefore it can be taken from the list. Two of the trains of the Canadian Pacific are likewise transcontinental and accordingly can also be taken from the list. Of the other two Canadian National trains, one is a fast express which connects with the maritime train and with the one to New York. The other is a slow local train calling at the various points between Montreal and Ottawa.
So far as the Canadian Pacific is concerned, their trains are in virtually the same position, with the exception that they have two lines, one the North Shore upon which two locals run in each direction. The others are practically the same, except that they have two transcontinentals which undoubtedly pick up traffic between these two cities, whereas the Canadian National has only one. There is, however, no doubt that throughout Canada between many cities there are opportunities for these two great railway systems to combine their passenger services at least to a certain extent and to effect savings by that kind of cooperation. Not long ago I travelled from Ottawa to my home in Fort William, and between Sudbury and Fort William there was on the train only one passenger besides myself. Hon. members know members of parliament do not pay much for their transportation, so that this service was not very remunerative from the point of view of passenger revenue.
There are other ways in which cooperation can be brought about, by the pooling of different services, by running rights over common trackage, and so forth. But dealing with

the question in a broader way, it is a most serious one impinging as it does on the whole financial structure of this country. At the same time largely because of its immensity, its importance, and its seriousness to this country it should be a non-controversial question so far as this house and even those outside of this house are concerned. I submit that there is no reason for party bias or party controversy in dealing with this question. It is too important and too serious for that type of treatment. In the recent hearings before the Senate committee on railways which considered this bill before it came to this house, the whole question was dealt with on a very high plane indeed. I had the pleasure of reading nearly four hundred pages of the evidence and I can say that the question was dealt with in a non-partisan and an entirely unbiased manner, and if I may respectfully make the suggestion I sincerely' hope that when this bill goes to the committee of the whole or is otherwise disposed of by this house it will be dealt with on exactly the same high plane, because I submit that this is no time for party strife, and I do not believe that the people of this country in these critical times, particularly having in mind the incidents of last week, are looking for party strife on a matter which is so serious to them as is this question.
The bill is a cooperative bill. It has for its purpose the cooperation to a large extent of the two railways. I repeat, there is nothing in it to cause anyone to fear that it may lead to the amalgamation of the two great railway systems of Canada because the whole trend and spirit of the bill, as well as every clause and letter of it, points to cooperation, and cooperation means, and can only mean, the working together of the two parties to an understanding, and in this case the two parties are the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. Without doubt this question, in spite of unemployment and the many other problems which Canada and the world at large have to face, is still the greatest problem confronting this dominion, and that is demonstrated by the heavy annual interest charges accruing to the investing public, in the United States to a great extent, on the bonds of the railway, two-thirds of which have been guaranteed by the Dominion of Canada, and for the other third of which this dominion is largely responsible-as the owners of the railway. The interest in 1932 was in round figures $58,000,000. In addition to that, as the house well knows, there is another item of interest which is piling up annually on the books of the company but

C IV.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Manion
is not shown in the public accounts of the dominion, amounting to §35,000,000 in round figures. That is interest owing to the government by the Canadian National Railways on past loans made by the government to the Canadian National Railways or to its subsidiary companies. None of that has been paid, and quite frankly I believe that no member of this house thinks that any of it ever will be paid.
There are other railways on this continent of course which are having difficulties, and that has often been pointed out. But the difference to us in this house and to the people of Canada is that these other railways, whether in Canada or the United States, are private corporations, and whatever difficulties they may get into, while they may have an indirect effect upon the financial structure and economic position of the country, yet they have not the same direct effect which the difficulties of -the Canadian National Railways have on our whole financial structure. In other words, the Canadian National Railways is directly our problem, and that problem is complicated by the fact that the Canadian National Railways, being a government road, has been for many years borrowing its money upon bonds, while many of the private companies, including the Canadian Pacific, have been raising the hundreds of millions of dollars, which they have put into roadbed and equipment, on stocks of one kind or another. On these stocks, fortunately for the privately owned railways, they may discontinue, and in most cases they have discontinued, the payment of dividends, whereas on the bonds of the Canadian National Railways the payment of interest to the investing public cannot be discontinued without repudiating our debt as a government. The fixed charges of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which as an institution is probably as valuable as the Canadian National Railways at any rate, amounted last year in round figures to $22,000,000, whereas the fixed charges of the Canadian National Railways, because of the reasons which I have just mentioned, amounted to $58,000,000.
In the United States practically all the private railway corporations have about the same proportion of bonds outstanding as against their book values as applies in the case of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The United States railways have a book value of 26 billion dollars, using the word billion in the American sense of one thousand millions. The bonded indebtedness against that 26 billion dollars in the United States is between 1.0 billion and 11 billion dollars, which is about 53719-176
the proportion of bonded indebtedness of the Canadian Pacific Railway as compared with its assets.
The whole situation is complicated, of course, to a still greater extent by the fact that traffic has decreased so very considerably in the last three or four years. In 1928 the gross revenues of the Canadian National Railways amounted to $304,000,000 while in 1932 they amounted to $161,000,000, or not very much more than half the total of the peak year. While at times we do remember that the peak year was a wonderful one from the standpoint of the Canadian National Railways inasmuch as in that year the railway paid the interest on its bonded indebtedness, which was unfortunately $15,000,000 or $16,000,000 less than the fixed charges in 1932, while it did that and had a couple of million dollars to spare, at the same time it had to borrow from the people of Canada, or have its bonds guaranteed by this dominion, to an amount of $26,000,000 in that year. So, even in its peak year, the road was a serious charge upon the people of this country.
I mention that merely to emphasize once again, as was emphasized not once but many times by the royal transportation commission at its hearings from coast to coast in this country, the seriousness of the whole situation, and to indicate why it is necessary for the Canadian National Railways, and the Canadian Pacific Railway indeed, to put into effect very drastic economies of all kinds. When you take into consideration the figures which I have mentioned, the interest owing by the Canadian National Railways, the competition in the last few years of motor vehicles, and finally the injurious effect upon all railways throughout the world of the widespread depression through which we have been passing, you will realize the reasons why the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway and all other railways on this continent and throughout the world find it necessary to put into effect great economies.
May I at once say this? In 1932 at any rate the Canadian National Railways in that regard did a splendid piece of work, probably unequalled, and I say that deliberately, by any other railway on the continent of North America. Let me give some proof in support of that statement. In 1932-the railway year for the Canadian National Railways is, as hon. gentlemen are aware, the calendar year-the gross revenues of the Canadian National Railways were down by $39,000,000 as compared with 1931. In the ordinary course of railway administration I am informed by the best authorities that when the revenues are down it is generally possible to decrease also

C .N.R ,-C P R. Bill-Mr. Manion
your expenses by from sixty to seventy per cent of the decrease in revenues, for of course there is the necessity for upkeep, maintenance, overhead and certain other general charges which cannot possibly be decreased as rapidly as the decrease which develops in revenues when conditions have- suddenly gone bad, as they have done throughout the world in the last four years. So taking from sixty to seventy per cent of the decrease in operating revenues of $39,000,000, there should have been a decrease in the operating expenses of the Canadian National Railways last year of between $25,000,000 and $27,000,000. But instead of that there was a decrease in operating expenses last year of $44,000,000, or 112 per cent, instead of the 60 per cent or 70 per cent that should have been expected, and is put into effect on most first class railways throughout the world in times of decreasing revenues. I say that is a remarkable showing oh the part of the Canadian National Railways, and to illustrate what it means I am going to quote statements by S. J. Hungerford himself who from time to time puts out statements for the information of the people of Canada. These statements concern the conditions on the Canadian National railways. On September 24 last, when these economies were being put into effect, Mr. Hungerford put out a statement. The statement was given to Mr. Paul Reading, who in turn quotes it in the Ottawa Citizen of September 4. Mr. Hungerford says:
Railway economy, he pointed out, was a progressive thing. It involved a constant increase in efficiency. Perhaps the best measure of recent improvement was that whereas the net operating revenue of the Canadian National in 1928, its peak year, had been roughly $56,000,0'00, the system as now organized could show a net of over S75.000.000 on the same volume of traffic as it handled in 1928.
In other words Mr. Hungerford pointed out that with the extreme type of economies which the Canadian National management and directorate had put into effect in the last year they could, with the same volume of traffic as 1928, have saved another $10,000,000.
It is sometimes feared that these economies have interfered with the efficiency of the Canadian National railways. In that connection, in the article which I have read, he spoke as follows:
From the standpoint of efficiency the system was in a strong position. "Never in its history" Mr. Hungerford asserted, "has this property been in such good physical condition or so well organized to handle traffic cheaply and efficiently as it is to-day."

Then in a statement which he gave to the press on January 3, 1933, he said the following:
In gauging measures of economy to meet declining revenues, the executives of a railway system must guard against jeopardizing the condition of the property. Facilities and equipment must be maintained on a standard of safety and efficiency. This factor has been carefully considered by the Canadian National Railways management and at the present time the property is in fit and proper condition to handle all traffic offering safely and efficiently.
That, I think, should set at rest any suggestion which occasionally is made to the effect that the efficiency of the railways is being in anyway sacrificed to economies. I may point out another statement Mr. Hungerford made to me personally only a few months ago. A statement had been made in another chamber by a very outstanding gentleman of that chamber that the employees of the Canadian National railways were going around fearfully expecting that when they went out in the morning they might have their positions, but when they came home at night they would not have them. I felt that was not a satisfactory position, and did not promote a satisfactory mental attitude on the part of the employees. With that in mind I talked the matter over with Mr. Hungerford, and he assured me at that time that outside of the necessary decreases due to decreasing business, the necessary contraction, on any large scale, had largely been accomplished.
May I at this point state that I wish to compliment very sincerely indeed not only Mr. Hungerford and the managing officers of the company, but all the men of the rank and file who have kept up their courage and who, through loyalty, have done their work faithfully and well for the Canadian National railways in very difficult times indeed. I wish to compliment them on the splendid esprit de corps they have shown. I do not believe I would be doing justice if at the same time I did not compliment the directors who, in the near future, will probably be replaced by the three trustees mentioned in the bill. The directors were appointed nearly three years ago. I wish to say here and now that the majority of them have done splendid work, have served loyally and well, and have given the very best they had in every possible way to help Mr. Hungerford and the management to bring about the results I have just indicated.
Because I believe the information will be of interest to the house, may I set out a few examples of the types of economies about which I spoke, and which I mentioned were

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Manion
specially put into effect by Mr. Hungerford and his managing officers. Not long ago he gave me a statement comparing the savings brought about by these special types of economies, showing the difference between the year 1932 and the year 1930. I did not think to ask him why he took one year instead of another. However he probably took 1932 because it was the last year, and I presume he took 1930 because it was at that time that the particular economies began. As a matter of fact in 1929 the decrease in revenues had not become very heavy, and I have no doubt the railway management of that day were probably hoping in the near future to get business back to normal. There is no doubt many people believed the depression would not last long. At any rate economies were not put into effect to any great extent until 1930.
The savings between 1930 and 1932 brought about by these special types of economies makes very interesting reading. For instance, of positions drawing salaries of $5,000 or over they have abolished fifty-six. Of positions drawing salaries between $3,000 and $5,000 they have abolished forty-seven. In other words among the supervisory officers of one kind and another they have eliminated one hundred and three who were receiving from $3,000, up. They claim that the efficiency of the road will not in any way be endangered by the elimination, and that the present staff could very well look after a very much greater volume of business than the railway is doing at the present time. I have no doubt as to the truth of that assertion. This elimination in salaries over $3,000 brought about a saving, in round figures of a little over $1,000.000,-[DOT] In addition; the reduction of salaries of those receiving salaries over $4,000, made a saving of over $900,000. Travelling expenses and club dues-but largely travelling expenses-were reduced by $850,000. Radio, medical services and advertising were cut by $1,250,000. Those four items alone make a total special saving of something over $4,000,000.
In addition to that however savings were made in passenger services which some years ago were thought to be necessary by all the railways on the continent. There had been growing up on this continent a very elaborate passenger service not only on the Canadian National railways but on all the other railways on the continent. In addition there was a very elaborate branch line service which, because of the popularity of motor cars, had been brought into the position of heavy losers. The lines and services throughout the country were surveyed, and between 1930 and 1932, eight million miles of passenger train services 53719-1765
have been eliminated. It has been estimated that this elimination has brought about a saving of a dollar a mile at least, in fact I have heard it estimated that the saving is as high as $1.50. However taking it at the rate of one dollar per mile the saving amounts to $8,000,000. Many of these savings that I have mentioned are permanent.
It is true that there have been strong protests made to the railway management and to myself personally about taking off services both on the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific railways. There seems to be a feeling throughout our country, I am sorry to say, that economies in the abstract are all to the good, but should not be applied to our own regions. I believe that is the feeling in the constituencies most hon. members represent. I presume all of us from time to time have received strenuous protests against some economies which were proposed to be put into effect. Apparently people believe we should economize, but should not carry out those economies in their constituencies, but always elsewhere. At the same time it should be pointed out that the people can hardly expect to be given elaborate train services when they are not patronizing these services, but are using automobiles instead of the trains.
There is another matter that I might mention in passing; I referred to radio savings. There is another saving which will be brought into effect in the near future, because it is intended within the next few days that the Canadian National will sell to the Dominion Radio Commission their whole radio plant, at a figure which has been decided upon. This will eliminate another heavy drain upon the Canadian National Railways, and as the staff is being taken over by the radio commission it will not mean any further increase of unemployment.
Would the minister permit a question? He gave the figures of 1932 as to reduction in operating expense of around $44,000,000. What would the reduction in revenue and in operating expense be for 1931?

I looked that up a day
or two ago, and while I cannot give the exact figures, there was no such saving as in 1932. The saving was in the neighbourhood of 50 per cent of the decrease in revenues from the previous year, instead of 112 per cent, as in 1932. Of course it is obvious that by no stretch of the imagination could a saving of 112 per cent of decreased revenues be made for many years. It can only be done at certain times. So that the saving between 1930

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Manion
and 1931 was very much less than the saving last year. I stated earlier in my remarks that the usual saving in cases like this was 60 to 70 per cent, so it was in the neighbourhood of the usual figure.

Will the minister give the
exact figures in committee?

Yes, I shall gladly do that.
There have been other improvements in management in the past year or so in which I think the house will be interested. I give them, I assure the house, in no spirit of criticism of the management or of anyone; I mention them merely because they are questions that have been discussed in the house at various times. For example, there has been a great improvement in regard to switching of estimates. I remember mentioning it here a year or so ago, and my right lion, friend the leader of the opposition supported me in my attitude, that switching of estimates should not be tolerated. Up to a year ago it was possible, for example, for the Canadian National Railways to have estimates passed through this house in their budget for huge amounts to be spent for certain capital expenditures in various parts of the country, and to switch them from that part to some other part and for a totally different purpose. For example, they might, and did on one occasion, if I remember aright, pass estimates for the building of a hotel in one section of the country and switch that money to the building of a branch line in another section. That is a power that no government, whether municipal, provincial or dominion, ever has had since constitutional government came into effect in this country. The railway in that respect had a power that no government had. In fact in 1931 the Canadian National switched amounts to the total of over $8,000,000. They are not permitted to do that any longer.
Another matter in which it was seen there was opportunity for improvement is this: There had grown up up in the Canadian National Railways the practice of permitting one officer, the chief engineer of the railway, to change the specifications or classifications on contract work so that the cost of the contract to the Canadian National might be varied by hundreds of thousands of dollars. Indeed, in one case into which I looked the cost had been increased by something like $600,000. This officer had the power to make changes involving huge sums without consulting even the president or other executive officers or the directors or any other group. I do not suggest for a moment that anything was done of an irregular character in that regard, but

I submit it is a greater power than should be in the hands of any one man of any corporation. I know of no other corporation, railway or otherwise, where one man had any such power. That has now been done away with. Another matter has been cleared up in which the fault I think, was due largely to the habit of architects, for example, of picking out what they think are the best lines of goods or materials and specifying those goods, irrespective of their origin, where the same type and quality of goods were being produced at an equal price in Canada. That habit had grown up in the Canadian National. In an investigation made at my request by the officers themselves, upon which they gave me a statement, it was found that forty per cent of all the specifications going out for materials for the building of hotels, terminals and so on were specifications of American goods. Without in any way thinking of criticizing American producers, I submit, and I know that members of the house will agree, that it is the duty of a Canadian institution supported by the money of the taxpayers to buy Canadian goods as far as possible.
May I, at this point, in regard to these various matters, again compliment the management and the directors who have cooperated so ably with the government in bringing about reform, which I think all hon. members of this house, of whatever party, will agree are advantageous to the Canadian National Railways.
It might be of interest to mention a few figures illustrating the decrease in traffic on all the railways on this half of the continent. Passengers carried in 1923 by the two great railway companies of this country amounted to 38,000,000, whereas in 1932 that number had decreased to less than half, about 18,000,000. Yet, during all that time both railways, and all railways on the continent, were spending huge sums in elaborate passenger services, and elaborate advertising for passenger traffic, which was the non-paying part of the railway business. I noted recently that Mr. Loree made the statement, which was widely quoted in the United States, that he thought too much money had been spent in past years on passenger traffic. That was seen by many men who were not railway men at all in this country in the last few years. During that time, when passenger traffic was decreasing so rapidly, there was a corresponding increase in the number of automobiles operating in Canada. In 1923 there were just over 500,000 automobiles of all kinds in use. and in 1931 just over 1.100.000, more than double the number, while the passengers in trains correspondingly decreased to one half.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Manion
It is well to remember that railways are absolutely necessary in a country such as Canada. With our immense distances, our huge quantities of bulk traffic, this country could hardly live without railways any more than the people of the country could live without air. We must have railways to carry our bulk traffic in such products as wheat, flour, cattle, coal, timber, and pulpwood. I mention those six products because in a recent report asked for by me I found that about two-thirds of the traffic on the Canadian National railways-and I presume it is true of the other railways in Canada-consisted of those six bulk products, products which could not possibly be handled by trucks or motor cars for our distances. So that I say the railways are an absolute necessity in the Dominion of Canada. That does not mean that it is our duty u any way to fetter the automobile progress of our country. We cannot hold back progress any more than we can hold back the tides. At the same time it is clear that the operation of money-making automobiles for private gain on public highways built out of the taxes of the people, a part of which are paid by the railways themselves, should be regulated in such manner as to provide at least fair competition to the railways. It is obvious that if we are to have fair competition for the railways without being unfair to the automobile, we should see that there ;s uniformity of regulation and taxation of road motor vehicles with a view to the equalization of conditions under which road and rail transport is carried on throughout the dominion. The motor cars of the country should pay at least a fair proportion of the upkeep and the interest on investment of the highways, and I feel that this can be brought about without in any way interfering with the progress of the automobile industry. The automobile can be and is now being made more complementary and supplementary to the railways than ever they have been in the past. The railways themselves have been very slow to realize the importance of utilizing automobiles to a greater extent than they have done in the past as feeders to their system. Only recently, it would seem, the railways have taken this into account. They seemed to have rested on their laurels, evidently under the impression that in the long run competition from the automobiles could not possibly handicap them, so that they ignored that competition which in the meantime has been rapidly increasing, with the result that the railways have been losing opportunities for making their business a profitable rather than a losing enterprise.
An arrangement has recently been made between Toronto on the east and Sarnia and Windsor on the west whereby the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National have undertaken the "pickup" system by means of which, at the Toronto end, hired automobiles -not purchased cars, so that there is no capital expenditure in this regard-are used to deliver goods to the trains, while at the other end automobiles are hired for the purpose of making deliveries to those to whom the goods are destined. It is an attempt, a somewhat belated attempt perhaps, on the part of the two railway companies to compete with the automobile in the carrying of traffic, and at the same time it is a very appropriate period in which to undertake a cooperative experiment, which we all trust will bring satisfactory results to the railway systems of Canada.
In this regard may I add that at the interprovincial conference held recently in this city an afternoon was devoted by the provincial and dominion representatives to a full discussion of the question of automobile competition with the railways, and it was decided on that occasion that my department should prepare a questionnaire to be sent out to the different provinces. When that questionnaire is returned with the appropriate answers from the different provinces it will be the duty of my department to endeavour so to coordinate the answers and afterwards to bring to Ottawa again the officials from the various provinces with the object of instituting more uniform taxation as well as more uniform charges and regulations with respect to motor traffic in competition with the railways. Incidentally, I may observe that within the last couple of weeks I have sent out the questionnaire, and during the discussion of the bill in the house I shall be glad to table it should anyone desire to see the document.
Another figure which is of interest with respect to our railways in Canada is the figure for coal consumption. In 1923 the two railways in Canada used 858,000.000 worth of coal, whereas in 1931 they used exactly one-half of that quantity, $29,000,000. That reduction indicates a greater operating efficiency on the part of the railways, showing that thej can get more out of the coal that they are using; it shows the effects of the depression on business, and it also shows the reason wh>
we are faced with the present difficulty oi having to look -after so many miners at botl ends of the country.
Both the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National Railways have been making commendable economies. Naturally I am

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Manion
more familiar with the economies of the Canadian National Railways than with those practised by the Canadian Pacific, inasmuch as the latter system, as hon. members know, is not under the necessity of reporting either to myself or to this parliament. I do believe however that the two railways have, broadly speaking, reached rock bottom; they have not attained the extreme limit, but they have accomplished nearly the limit, with the exception of certain considerable economies which might still be made as a result of that greater cooperation between the two systems which will be brought about when the present measure becomes law. The foundations have been laid by both railways, and indeed probably by all the railways on this continent, so that they will be in a position when there is a revival of business throughout the continent and the world at large, to come back very rapidly. I believe they will profit by some of the painful experiences they have had to endure during the years of the crisis. I may add, with respect to these rather painful economies that have been made by the Canadian National Railways, that when the three trustees are appointed they should, if they show the proper courage and good judgment, be able to keep that system on the right track, if I may use an appropriate metaphor, so far as efficient and economical management is concerned. It may be added of course that unless there is that business revival which we all look for in the near future there can be no solution of our transportation difficulties throughout this continent. There is however every expectation, particularly after the events of the last week, that we shall in the near future experience that revival in business which we confidently anticipate.
Recently in the United States the bondholders of private railways in that country, who consist very largely of insurance companies, savings banks and trust companies- in other words, the repositories of the savings of the people, holding about seventy per cent of the bonds of the American railways-* got together and appointed a commission on something of the basis of the royal commission which was appointed in this dominion. They appointed the late Mr. Calvin Coolidge as chairman, Mr. Alfred Smith, Mr. Baruch, and two other business men whose names escape me for the moment. These gentlemen reported after a thorough investigation of the situation that, with the economies that have been put into effect on the railways in the American republic, a twenty per cent increase in traffic would serve to bring

their railways back to a good revenue position. I do not believe that twenty per cent of an increase in traffic would restore our railways to a normal condition, but I do think that fifty per cent of an increase would go a long way towards getting them out of the slough of despond into which they have sunk; I think that such an increase would bring them back to something like a hopeful position. Everyone who is reasonable feels that we may well entertain hopes for the future without smashing the whole economic machine which has served us for so many years. When a man has an automobile which has been giving good service for years, he does not, if it goes out of order, take an axe or burglar's tools if he wants to repair it; he gets someone to help him to get it back into running order. Now that should be our attitude towards the economic system under which we live. People generally realize, I believe, that the conditions under which our railways, our agriculture and the whole of our commercial enterprises are operating at the present time are world conditions. That is clearly understood, I think, for people realize that no individual nation or leader alone can restore conditions to normal. In other words, there must be international cooperation on such questions as international indebtedness, world trade barriers and primary commodity prices. These three questions particularly must be studied. If we are to get primary commodity prices back to anything like a reasonable basis, it must be the result of some international conference. The restoration of primary commodity prices to something like a reasonable level, and the stabilizing of those prices at that level, would not only lessen to a large extent the debts of individuals and nations, but would bring back that purchasing power which is necessary not only to provide business for the railways but to further business generally.
I had that well illustrated a few days ago, when I made it my endeavour to find out how shipments of wheat compared in the last year with one of the previous years considered as an outstanding period in the progress of the railways. I found that in the year 1929, 4,600,000 tons of wheat was shipped on the railways, and in 1932, 5,300,000 tons, an increase of 700.000 tons in 1932 as compared with 1929; yet the gross revenues of the Canadian National Railways were down in 1932 as compared with 1929 as by $125,000,000.

Not on
wheat alone.

No, on the total revenues.
I mention this to my hon. friend because it has been the conviction of many of us-I must confess it was my own conviction-that grain traffic was the paying traffic of the railways. As a matter of fact, it was not so much the wheat and grain traffic that was the paying traffic for the railways as the fact that the people of the west were selling their products at a reasonable price and had the money with which to purchase goods from some other section of the country, thus providing return traffic; and that total traffic brought about the prosperity of the railways.

Could the minister give
us the earnings on the wheat traffic as well as the tonnage carried during the two years he mentioned?
I have not that information under my hand but I shall be glad to furnish it during the committee stage of the bill.
I submit that the earnings would not be larger even though the tonnage was greater if the haul were shorter.

There is something in
that because a larger proportion of the wheat has been going via Vancouver which is a shorter haul. However, the 700,000 tons additional in 1932 over 1929 would balance the shorter haul. It is the low purchasing power of the western farmer due to the low prices he is receiving for his grain which causes his inability to purchase the goods of the eastern producer. This in turn prevents the prosperity of the railways as well as of the industrial plants of the country. There is no purchasing power, no effective demand.
Hear, hear.
I hope that my hon. friend who says " hear, hear," does not imagine that that thought belongs only to our friends over there.

Does the minister intend
to move to refer this bill to the railway committee?

I am coming to that point.
I submit that the railways as well as the world in general can be more hopeful today than they have been for many days past or even for years, certainly for many months. The time seems opportune for a recovery of world conditions. We are all looking forward to a world economic conference from which, if matters are dealt with in a proper cooperative and international manner, it is hoped world recovery will come. When that recovery does take place, as I sinoerely believe it
will in the near future, then the railways as well as the other industries will come back to prosperity. I submit that the outlook for the railways is far from hopeless, provided always that the trustees to be appointed are careful to carry on the management in an economical manner and provided also that there is at the same time a revival of trade in Canada and throughout the world.
In connection with the question asked by the hon. member for Kenora (Mr. Heenan) as to whether or not it is my intention to submit this bill to the committee on railways, shipping and telegraph lines, I should like to say that it is my intention to suggest submitting it to a committee of the whole house. These matters have been dealt with very fully by the royal commission. This commission travelled from coast to coast and took evidence from all those who desired to submit evidence. They heard provincial authorities, railway officers, railway employees-public bodies and individuals-any who felt that they had some contribution to make to the solution of the question. In addition, the Senate committee heard further witnesses, most of whom had appeared before the royal commission, and it is my opinion that it is not necessary to go to the trouble and expense of hearing these witnesses over again.
In closing may I say that while the principles of this bill are supported in entirety by the government, the government has no strong feeling in regard to matters of detail. We will welcome suggestions from any part of the house with regard to contributions as to details, but at the same time we feel that the royal commission has made a most careful study of the whole question and its submissions should be given fair trial by the people of Canada. After the money and time spent upon this royal commission, if proper heed were not given to its recommendations, the people of Canada might feel that its efforts had been wasted.
The minister mentioned the decrease in passenger traffic from 1923 to 1932 as being some 18,000.000; has he the corresponding figures for freight tonnage?

I have the gross figures
under my hand but I do not wish to give them at this moment. I shall be very glad to give any information asked for when the bill is in committee.
I should like to repeat, and I do it most respectfully, that I believe this whole question is so wrapped up with the future development of this country that it should be dealt with on the high plane of strong

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Euler
Canadianism rather than in any sense of partyism. I trust that I have said nothing which might be considered as being unfairly critical of any body or group. In making my remarks I have endeavoured to occupy the same plane which I am suggesting hon. members should occupy in dealing with this bill.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to follow the minister in reviewing the financial operations of the Canadian National Railways. He has the advantage of his position in that his department can supply him with figures which are not so readily available to myself. I intend to address myself to the merits of the bill itself. May I say to the minister that as one who sits on this side of the house I can congratulate him upon the moderation of his remarks. Parliament and the country generally may be congratulated upon the optimism with which he views the future. I am afraid, however, that I cannot quite follow him when he states that a more or less mathematical miracle has been performed in the saving of 112 per cent. I used to regard 100 per cent as the limit of what could be done in anything. If the government could make the same saving in its other operations we would soon be out of the difficulties in which we find ourselves.
The minister made reference to the present condition of the Canadian National Railways and he stated that Mr. Hungerford, the present president of the road, declares that the railways are in perfect physical condition. I am glad to hear that, but would like to say, without arousing any recriminations, that admirable condition of the Canadian National Railways was not brought about in one or two years; it is the result of the good work done in years gone by.
It is gratifying that it has been possible in the last year or two to effect the great savings which the minister has mentioned to-day. However, it would not be fair to assume that such savings can be always effected in periods of prosperity. While it is true that great expenditures were made during the prosperous years of 1927 and 1928, I think it must be realized that it is not possible to effect in periods of prosperity the savings which are sometimes enforced upon us during periods such as we now have. Commercial and industrial enterprises have found it necessary to effect economies just as has been done in the case of the national railway. I do not say this by way of criticism but rather that no wrong conclusion may be drawn from the minister's observations.

As has been stated, this bill is the direct outcome of the recommendations contained in the report of the royal commission on railways and transportation, and it might be regarded as being quite in order to discuss at this time some of the features of that report. It is not my intention to do so other than to say that while I disagree emphatically with some of the opinions and inferences that are drawn in the report, I am wholly in accord with the chief purposes that the government desires to attain in the bill now before the house. I do not suppose the government anticipates or expects that this bill will cure all the evils from which the railways are suffering. If the bill carries in its present form, so much after all depends upon the good faith, ability and public spirit, if you like, of the men who will be placed in charge of those railways, that one can only say that the best results can be obtained if those people act efficiently, in a spirit of good faith and with an eye only to the good of the Canadian National Railways.
I support the second reading of the bill chiefly for four reasons. In the first place, the integrity and identity of the Canadian National Railways is preserved. I listened with a good deal of satisfaction to the assurances given by the minister that there was not in the mind of the government-and I may say I do not suspect them-any thought whatsoever that the provisions of this bill might be used for the purpose of amalgamating the Canadian National Railways with the Canadian Pacific Railway. I do say this, however, that while it may be quite true there i3 in the bill nothing which permits amalgamation, that fact might be made just a little more clear by the insertion of a clause making it unmistakable where parliament stands in the matter. I support the bill for the second reason that the establishment of a small body of trustees of three or four, as the case may be, will promote efficiency in the conduct of the Canadian National Railways. There is a third advantageous provision in the bill if it is properly carried out, and if the government would consent perhaps to make some slight changes in the method of appointing the board of trustees, this might minimize to a very great degree the harmful influences that may be exercised in a political way. Fourth, the bill provides a plan whereby it is hoped savings may be effected; that waste that has come because of the severe competition existing between the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National railways may be eliminated. These advantages, in my opinion, are thoroughly worth while.

C.N.R -C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Euler
The railway situation, as has been pointed out by the minister, is assuredly sufficiently serious to be a challenge to the patriotism, if you will, and the sense of public duty and responsibility of every member of this house. The reason for the condition in which the railways find themselves, are fairly obvious to most of us, although there may be some differences of opinion. First, there is the depression which has affected all lines of business and perhaps more particularly the railways. Then there is the contraction of trade, the lack of freight to carry over the railways, the wasteful competition between the two great railway systems and the competition with which the railways have been obliged to deal so far as another method of transportation is concerned, that of the truck and automobile. I would second the wish of the minister when he says that he hopes we may approach this whole question in a spirit free of prejudice, free of partisanship, and with the single purpose of cooperation in the national duty of doing what we can to relieve the country of this burden which has been placed upon us by reason of the depression in the business of the Canadian National Railways and throughout the country generally. The Senate have shown us a very good example; they have discussed and dealt with the question on a patriotic and purely business basis, hoping to do what they can in the interests o>f Canada itself. I might, if I cared, refer to a few exceptions to that, but I shall refrain from doing so.
In addition to the matters mentioned, I would not forget that there are in the bill other provisions which are of some importance, but quite subordinate to the four I have enumerated. The bill provides for a continuous audit, auditors to be appointed by parliament and reports to be made by them direct to parliament. It provides for the separation of the chairmanship of the board from the presidency of the railroad, and I shall have something more to say with regard to that. It provides that all bond issues shall be made by the federal government rather than by the railway itself. It provides further that there shall be no more funding of deficits. These matters are not new and I imagine they are placed in the bill not entirely by reason of the recommendations made by the royal commission, but because our parliamentary committee on national railways and shipping in the past has made these very recommendations coupled with the further one, that we are in favour of a reduction in the number of those who are to form the board of management of the Canadian National Railways.	.
I should like now to discuss the three parts of the bill. The first provides for the substitution of a small board of trustees for the present cumbersome board of management of seventeen, if I may call it such without casting any reflections upon its present members. I believe, as a business principle, a small body of men will do better work than a very large body such as we have. Let me say this further: Perhaps the government will accept a suggestion that I am going to make a little later. I believe by the composition of this board, it might be possible, as I have said before, to exercise political patronage and political influence upon the conduct of the railway. I have never favoured the appointment of the former boards upon the basis of political preference, I am not criticizing any one government more than another. Quite frankly, I believe it has never been in the interests of the Canadian National Railways that in the appointment of that board of sixteen or seventeen directors, any consideration should have been given to the political persuasion or complexion of the members of the board, or to geographical considerations. If there is a small board of trustees of three, although my mind is open as regards increasing that to five, it will be possible to eliminate from the appointments the matter of allotting a member to British Columbia, or the prairie provinces, or Nova Scotia, or any other province. Appointments should be made with certain qualifications in view: first, with reference to the ability of the men who shall be appointed; second, that they shall be men of integrity-and that goes without saying; third, that they shall possess something of the spirit of public service-that is important-and finally-and this is almost of paramount importance; at least it seems of great importance to me- that the men who will be selected as the board of trustees shall be men who believe in the principle of public ownership.
I approve entirely the provision which states that the board shall be responsible to parliament; that may mean responsible to the government, because the government, after all, controls parliament. I believe also it is a good step that the president of the road, who will be the chief operating officer, should be appointed by the board of trustees and responsible to that board alone. Again, although it is perhaps not of great importance, it does not seem appropriate that the chief operating officer of the road should be designated by the name "president." It would be more appropriate and descriptive if you called him the general manager of the road, and the term "president" could be much

more fittingly applied to the chairman of the board of trustees. I merely make that suggestion in passing. I believe also that if you have only three trustees, all the trustees should give their whole time to the work, and that not only the chairman but all should be well paid; and if there are only three, or even five, the majority should rule, and the chairman should not have supreme authority.
Just a word with regard to the method of appointment. The1 initial board which will replace the present board is to be appointed by the governor in council, by the government itself. Succeeding vacancies, no matter how caused, by the effluxion of time, by resignation, if you like, by the death of a member of the board, shall be made on an entirely different plan. These succeeding vacancies shall be filled from a panel of eight men, which panel is to be selected by a body consisting of the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, the chief of the Exchequer court and the two remaining trustees. I have no fault to find with that because if it is carried out in good faith it will be possible to give at least the impression which I hope would be based on fact that politics does not enter into the appointment of these men. But I would point out this anomaly. While these succeeding vacancies are to be filled from a panel of eight men selected as I have indicated by this group of four, the government thereby recognizing the principle of nonpartisanship in the composition of that panel and in the appointment of the board of trustees, if that principle is sound in the filling of succeeding vacancies, it ought to be just as sound in the appointment of the original board of trustees. The suggestion I desire to make is this, that this first board of trustees, which appointments the government will make, shall be appointed from a panel of eight selected by the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners and the chief of the Exchequer court, and two others as a result of a consultation of the members of this house, all parties included. If the government would do that, I think they would give the impression. and honestly I think, that it is their real desire to remove as far as possible from the administration of the Canadian National Railways political influence and political pull, if I may put it in that way.
We have a precedent for that. When the chief electoral officer of Canada was appointed some years ago, the then Prime Minister consulted with those then leading the opposition and an agreement was reached, and the gentleman who was chosen as a result of that consultation served in a manner that was entirely satisfactory. I just want to impress that once
[Mr. Euler.l
again on the government. If the government sincerely desires, and I do not question their motives for one moment, that the people of Canada shall be impressed with the fact that in the conduct of the Canadian National Railways politics does not enter, and it is a bad thing I will say when politics does enter into business, I think they might very readily accept the suggestion I have made or something similar which would eliminate as far as possible the suggestion of political influence in the appointment of the initial board of trustees.
With regard to part 2 of the bill, I may say that I regarded that as of relatively little importance. It seemed to me that it expresses what is sometimes spoken of as merely the pious wish that the railways should cooperate in the cutting out of useless expenditures, with a solemn injunction to them to do so. But the teeth which are in the bill to implement that pious wish are to be found in part 3.
Before leaving part 2 of the bill I want to make a reference to the matter of amalgamation. The minister assured us during the course of his address that the government had not the slightest desire that anything in this bill should be used for the purpose of merging the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway, and I accept his word for that. But there was in the original draft of the bill that went to the Senate a clause which has since been elmin-ated, and which reads as follows-it was subsection 2 of section 16:
But nothing herein shall be taken to authorize any amalgamation of any National company with any Pacific company.
I have not followed throughout the proceedings of the Senate committee, but I am curious to know why that clause was cut out.

If my hon. friend will permit me to answer now, I did not know that the clause had been cut out until very recently and then I made inquiries from the leader in the Senate and others and found that it was cut out because it was considered as surplus words, that there was nothing in the act leading towards amalgamation or that authorized amalgamation, and that therefore the words were not necessary.
I think I heard the Prime Minister say that it was foolish to insert that clause.

by a rather prominent barrister in the city of Toronto. I shall not read the whole of his statement, but he said in part:
Under the act as it now stands, it is possible to legally disembowel, dismantle and ruin the Canadian National Railways unless a plain, unambiguous clause or section is inserted and made part of the act, preventing and prohibiting any amalgamation, merger or transfer of any of the funds, revenues, business, properties and assets of the Canadian National Railways to or with the Canadian Pacific Railway.
I bring that up merely for the purpose of ensuring that there can be no doubt whatsoever with regard to it. There are some people-I believe there are some on this side of the house as well as throughout the country -who do have the fear that under this bill it may be possible by certain action to effect amalgamation of the Canadian National with the Canadian Pacific, and I would ask the minister, the Prime Minister, and the government whether it would not be worth while, in order to remove the fears of these people, to reinsert this clause that was deleted. Lastly I come to part 3 of the bill. Part 3 which deals with what is sometimes called the compulsory cooperation of the two railway systems. It is intended to eliminate wasteful competition and to save money for both railway companies I suppose, but primarily for the Canadian National Railways. I may say in passing, Mr. Speaker, that I think it is the duty of this parliament, when endeavouring to do something for the Canadian National Railways, to do no injustice to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Ordinarily I do not believe a great deal in compulsion, and when I first read the recommendation of the commission in that respect, and first saw the bill as introduced into the Senate, I had no great confidence that this compulsory cooperation would be very successful or that the clause would be very valuable.
I am not sure that I have changed my mind. Compulsion and cooperation do not go very well together. Cooperation implies voluntary action, not compulsion. But it may be that in the public interest compulsion sometimes becomes necessary. If it does become necessary, and the results one hopes to attain through compulsion can be obtained in no other way and are for the general good of the Canadian people as well as for the good of the Canadian Pacific Railway, then I believe I might strain a point and support even that.
One further word vrth regard to amalgamation: The minister referred to the term to-day, and I have mentioned it myself. It is idle at this time to argue concerning amalgamation. For the time being at least I think it is set aside, and I would not bring it up now were it not for the intensive campaign or propaganda that is being carried on by certain people who advocate the merging of the Canadian National with the Canadian Pacific railways. The president of the Canadian Pacific Railway-and I do not blame him for his activity, because he is acting in the interests of his shareholders-is of the opinion that the only solution to the railway problem of Canada lies in the amalgamation of the two roads and, of course, by preference, amalgamation under private ownership. A-t the risk of being tedious and saying something I have said in the house before, may I repeat that so long as ten years ago I suggested to the then government that it might be advisable to canvass the whole railway situation with a view to possible amalgamation. I believe everybody recognized at that time that there was a great deal of waste and duplication of services, and some of 'the difficulties mentioned by the minister this afternoon.
I made the statement then, and had it on very good authority, that at least $75,000,000 a year could be saved by a merging of the two roads. My suggestion was not acted upon at the time. I made it again last year, and the year before. Now we have Mr. Beatty of the Canadian Pacific Railway making the same claim-although it is contradicted by the president of the Canadian National Railways-to the effect that $75,000,000 a year could be saved by amalgamation. If that had been true, and if action had been taken ten years ago, by this time we would have saved an amount equal to about one-third of the national debt. I agree with Mr. Beatty that we could effect a tremendously greater saving by amalgamation than by any such plan as provided in part III of the bill. I realize it is impossible to do anything in that connection at this time, and I know further, the arguments that are levelled constantly against amalgamation. May I say, lest I embarrass
