hon. members on this side of the house, that on this point I speak for myself and for nobody else, knowing full well thait many hon. members who sit about me disagree with me at times.
That is a wise thing to do.
That's playing safe.

I speak entirely for myself, and for no one else. I should like to answer the argument which is brought constantly and which, so far as I am concerned, has no force, namely that in all cases monopoly is bad. I say without, fear of successful contradiction that there is a world of difference between privately and publicly owned monopolies. The objectives in the two systems are entirely different. In private monopoly the motive is profit; in a public monopoly the motive is the best of service at cost. In a public monopoly no good can be done by any one trying to take advantage of the public, because the public itself is the owner of the monopoly.
The suggestion of an amalgamation is not particularly new, and at the moment I am not urging it. But even in France, in view of the fact that privately owned roads are losing millions and scores of millions of dollars, we find the Minister of Public Works making a suggestion that the state take over the railways. In Italy the roads are owned by the state. Those roads some years ago were handed over on a leasehold to a private railway concern. The result was that there was constant bickering; the railway company was constantly complaining that it could not get the money necessary to carry out capital expenditures to put the roads in condition. The government and the people complained about the service, and finally the state took the railways back under state control. There is state control in Germany and Australia, and at the present time there is a movement in the United States whereby the multitudinous number of roads in that country are gradually being combined under four great systems. Possible amalgamation may take place later on.
I know that at the moment there is no use arguing in favour of amalgamation, because at this time I do not believe the people of Canada desire it. I do say, however, that if amalgamation does come the people of Canada will not stand for a private monopoly of the -railway business. If we are to have amalgamation it must be publicly owned.
[Mr. Euler.l
There are just two other points I should like to mention in connection with the campaign which has been carried on by the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway. He has stated in his speeches that in the last few years the country has suffered a loss of about $85,000,000 a year on Canadian National Railways account. While in a sense true, that statement is misleading because it includes the $35,000,000 interest on the debt which was created, very largely before the roads were taken over. It includes the advances that were made by the Dominion government to those railways which now comprise the Canadian National railway system, an amount of money which in my opinion should have been written off long ago, an amount which if written off would not save the Canadian people from the payment of interest, but at least would put the principle of public ownership on a basis where it could fairly be compared with a system under private ownership.
When the suggestion is made that the Canadian National Railways should merge with the Canadian Pacific Railway I believe the impression is conveyed, whether intentionally or not, that we would then be rid of the tremendous loss which we suffer in connection with the Canadian National system. When that is suggested I believe the Canadian peo-ple would do well to turn to the words of Mr. Beatty,, as they appear at page 914 of the proceedings of the royal commission. They are as follows:
I also dismiss the possibility of a change involving the transfer of the government lines, subject to their existing obligations, to a private company. No private corporation could assume the enormous obligations which the government railways are under. If it did, the project could never be made to yield a profit and the company would find itself unable to finance the undertaking.
In other words, if we did hand the Canadian National Railways over to the Canadian Pacific Railway we would still have to pay the interest on a large part of our obligations because, as Mr. Beatty said, the Canadian Pacific Railway would not assume them. We would be in the position that the Canadian Pacific Railway would probably have a profitable enterprise and the Canadian people would still be paying the shot by way of interest on liabilities.
To the relief of the house I am about to discontinue my remarks in connection with amalgamation, and shall consider part III of the bill. The purpose of part III, as the minister has said, is a worthy one. It provides for the elimination of wasteful com-

C.NM.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Hackett
petition, covering joint use of terminals, running rights, joint use of tracks, new line and duplication of old lines, abandonment of lines, and the pooling of freight and passenger traffic. If one road makes a suggestion that the other road agree to eliminate a service which appears to be extravagant and wasteful, and the other road refuses to accede to the wishes of the first road, there is provision for the appointment of an arbitral tribunal. A tribunal is appointed for each separate dispute. The point I would like to make, in connection with these tribunals, apart from the extreme degree of authority given to the chairman of the tribunal, is that the railways alone can initiate the arbitral tribunal-I think I am correct-that no one else, no matter how far the public interests were prejudiced, can initiate an arbitral tribunal. The chairman always is the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and there is one representative of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and one of the Canadian National. The chairman is supreme, because decisions cannot be made without his consent. Naturally each representative of the railway would adhere to his own view, the chairman gives the decision, so that in effect the chairman is the one who makes the decision. His decision is final; there is no appeal from it.
My criticisms in connection with the arbitral tribunal plan are these: first too much power in the hands of one man; second-this criticism is made by others and I do not place so much stress upon it, but it is made by the Canadian Pacific Railway-compulsion is unfair to the Canadian Pacific; and third that the public is not protected; and that is the strongest criticism that I have to make. It should be possible for the public to initiate an arbitral tribunal. I make the suggestion for the consideration of the government and the house, that so far as the one man power is concerned, that could be avoided if additional powers, such as are given now to the arbitral tribunal, were vested in the present Board of Railway Commissioners, and that a majority there should decide. With regard to the matter of compulsion I might make this suggestion for what it is worth, that you would get rid of that factor if these disputes were referred to a body similar to that which acts under the Industrial Disputes Act. Their decisions are not compulsory, but usually, if they are fair, and I think ordinarily they are, public opinion would see that they were brought into force.
In conclusion I would say that, after all, the working out of the provisions of this bill will succeed exactly in the degree that it is done in good faith. If a good board is
appointed, a capable board, non-political, a board that is not concerned with anything but the good of the railways, and that believes in the principle of public ownership, I think good may result. If I thought for one moment-I do not-that it is the intention of the government or anyone else that this bill shall lend itself to the amalgamation of the roads without the consent of this house or the people of Canada, I certainly should oppose the second reading of the bill. I prefer to believe that the government, that parliament, that the trustees to be appointed, are sincere in an effort to do what can be done to relieve the people of Canada of the burden now oppressing both railways. I shall therefore vote for the second reading of the bill, reserving always the right to make such suggestions or amendments as may seem desirable when the bill goes into committee of the whole house.
Mr. JOHN T. HACKETT (Stanstead): The discussion on this bill falls within rather narrow limits. The remarks of the hon. gentleman who moved the second reading (Mr. Manion), as well as of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) who has just spoken, show that the bill will have substantial support from both sides of the house. I do not think any useful purpose can be served by retelling the long story which brought about the investigation and the findings which underlie this bill. My hon. friend from North Waterloo is an ardent and consistent believer in public ownership. He could not therefore refrain from inviting the government to select for trustees under the act adherents of his own economic theory. He is hopeful that men who believe in the principle of public ownership shall be selected for these very important offices. That probably is a natural suggestion from one who entertains his views. But he surely does not expect those who entertain contrary views to be very much moved by the suggestion. He has told us that railroads are publicly owned in other parts of the world; he mentioned Germany, where I think public ownership was adopted for military purposes. He mentioned France, where the roads are with some exceptions publicly owned, to the great dismay of the population and the disarray of their finances. In Australia the railroads are publicly owned. Almost every possible plan of administration has been tried, and the railroads continue to be, as with us, the principal burden and item in public expenditures. My hon. friend from North Waterloo wishes that politics, which he considers a baneful influence in the administration of railways, should be 'banished therefrom.

C.N.R.-C.P.R- Bill-Mr. Hcickett
I think many of us share that wish, but after all when ownership resides in the public I think that the owner, expressing his views through the politician, his mandatory and spokesman, will inevitably and always find a voice. The hon. member for North Waterloo warned the house that he was speaking for himself alone,
I too can say that as far as I am concerned I am not sure that if public ownership is to prevail it will not bring fewer evils in its train, if administered honestly and openly, as the other public undertakings of this country. We have got into serious trouble with our railways largely because, being publicly owned and subject to political influence, we have endeavoured to shield them and ourselves from reality by putting them under what is called independent administration. I do not believe it is possible to have administration which is entirely free from the influence of ownership. So long as we have public ownership of railways, public men are bound to exercise a certain influence over their administration no matter what safeguards surround it. I will ask the house, taking it for granted that a tremendous debt has been placed upon the country as a result of the public ownership and administration of the railways, whether this debt would have been as large, whether our position would have been as perilous if these roads had been administered-with all the ills and evils of partisanship and politics-by a responsible minister of the crown who was subject to the curiosity, to the criticism and control of a vigilant parliamentary opposition. I doubt it very much indeed.
Be that as it may, my task is to discuss very briefly the three or four salient aspects of this legislation. The train of events leading up to the legislation is well known to the house. We have invested in railways $2,600,000,000 and, roughly, half of that amount is owing to the public. The interest on the amount that is owing to the public is about $60,000,000 a year. To find the money necessary to refund and retire maturing obligations; to find the money necessary for capital expenditure, for interest on obligations, and latterly for income deficits, we have borrowed. We have borrowed continuously and consistently until, as I said a moment ago, the amount now owing to the public by the railways is about $1,300,000,000. A very substantial portion of this amount is guaranteed by the government of Canada. About two or three hundred millions are not contractually guaranteed by the government but are effectually guaranteed inasmuch as the debt is^ a lien upon the entirety of the enterprise which is operated as a whole.

The full cost of railway transportation must be paid by the classes served, by the taxpayers of the time, or charged to the future with compound interest. To spread this cost over a long period in the name of constructive benevolence is the course which we have followed until now. We are told that our borrowing power is exhausted; in fact, there is in the bill a provision which .makes it illegal to borrow for the purpose of paying income deficits. The royal commission was appointed to find a solution for this problem. It was appointed to examine the whole transportation problem and if possible to find a way out which would relieve the country and in particular the taxpayer. After considering the problem in all its aspects it brushed aside the possibility of amalgamation either by purchase or by lease. The reason given was that amalgamation was inopportune at the moment. Another reason given was that it would be unwise to formulate in a moment of stress a definite policy which might be unsuited to more normal times. That leads one inevitably to the conclusion that this proposal embodied in the report of the commission and reproduced in the bill is but a temporary expedient and does not contain any final disposition of the railway problem.
The bill aims at bringing some relief to the Canadian taxpayer and it finds that the only way that it can do this is by reducing the cost of operation. It cannot reduce the debt; it cannot increase the earning power; so that the only method left is to reduce the cost of operating of the roads. It proposes to do this in a hitherto untried way. Had amalgamation taken place either under private or public ownership, the owner would then have reduced the railway system to the size, needs and capacity to pay of the Canadian people. This bill, while maintaining the identity of ownership of both the privately and publicly owned roads, attempts to bring about this elimination of unnecessary equipment, mileage and service, by a method which, so far as my investigation has carried me, has never been tried before. The method is euphemistically called cooperation, but it is a type of cooperation which is to be coerced if it is not voluntarily entered into. I cannot see how either party mentioned in the bill can be expected voluntarily to lop off large portions of its system. It is admitted that we have too much mileage; it is admitted that we have too many trains, and it is admitted as a consequence we have too many men in the employ of the railroad companies and that, therefore, it is necessary to reduce the mileage in

operation and to eliminate the service and equipment which duplicates in any form that given by the other line. The tribunal will have not only the right but the duty of determining where this elimination can most properly take place. Naturally the Canadian National will not be disturbed very much by_ the exercise of these arbitrary powers; it is owned by the people of Canada and indirectly administered by the government of Canada and the creation of a tribunal by parliament will subject the Canadian National to no new control or master. But it is not so with the Canadian Pacific; that road will find itself subjected to the rulings of a tribunal which will have the right to say: this portion of your road you shall no longer use; this station shall be invaded by your erstwhile rivals, or this ticket office shall be closed. In other words, the government will be actually controlling private enterprise and stating how far it may exercise the rights which up until now have been limited only by the statute of its incorporation and by the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. This is a new principle applied to the business life of our country, and whether or not it will be applied tomorrow to the operators of cotton mills, to the growers of wheat or to other branches of our financial, industrial and economic life remains to be seen. It may even contain the germ of the new order toward which all eyes are turned. However, it is an experiment and an experiment which cannot be looked upon with equanimity by both parties affected by the bill. The one will remain under the control of its owners, the other passes under the control of an alien power.
Can this legislation remedy the railway ills of the country? By cooperation, voluntary or coercive, by the elimination of duplication and the loss and waste incident to competition, can we hope that the revenues from the Canadian National Railways will be equal to the carrying charges of the debt which now weighs upon the Canadian National Railways and their owners, the people of Canada? The minister has told us of the great effort which has been made by the officers of the Canadian National to reduce the expenses of that road. I am not in a mood to criticize or to carp, but if the expenses could be reduced by 112 per cent, the road must have been generous if not lavish in its expenditures in better days.
Even though this bill bring all the relief that its most ardent adherents hope for, the railway problem will not be solved. Let no one be lulled into the belief that the passage of this bill will extricate us from the diffi-
Bill-Mr. Hackett
culties incident to the ownership and administration of this vast transportation system. Before we have disposed of the problem not only will highway traffic have to be brought under control, as suggested this afternoon by the minister, but a closer investigation will have to be conducted into the competition offered by our canals. We have spent millions, yes hundreds of millions upon our canal system. We permit foreign boats to leave the port of Vancouver, let us say, go through the Panama canal where they pay tolls, come up the St. Lawrence river and through our canals, which are toll free, and penetrate 2,000 miles inland in competition with our railways. I submit that that is a type of competition rather difficult to justify, especially in these days when the Canadian taxpayer is under such a heavy burden.
There is another aspect of the railway situation which the royal commission seems to have overlooked, that as the relationship between the railroads and the railway employees. I am aware that the railway employees are highly organized, that they are a very valuable element of our population, intelligent, industrious and law abiding; but the fact remains that the scale of wages and the operating rules under which they ply their trade are unusual and exceptional. If members of certain branches of the running trades drive an engine a hundred miles in a couple of hours they have done a day's work. If a crew is called out for a short time, again it is treated as if it had done a full day's work., I am not anxious to take away from the Canadian railway employee anything to which he is fairly entitled, but if this problem is as serious as we are told on all sides and as we have been told by the royal commission itself that it is, it seems to me that we shall have to scrutinize more closely the conditions of labour as well as those of the pay of that vast army of railway employees.
There are aspects of the bill which do not greatly appeal to me. The centralized power in a board of three trustees has elements of strength; it also has elements of peril. In a moment of stress and of emergency it may well be that a small and highly concentrated board of this type can render useful service. But one of the great ills of the years just passed has been the tendency to merge, centralize and concentrate, with the result that the outlying districts have been neglected for the big centres, the cities, rvith the consequence that the strong have become too strong and the weak have become weaker.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Heaps
I fear that in this highly centralized organization there are possibilities of trouble which, in other times at least, should be avoided.
The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) made some reference to the fact that the president was supreme in the arbitral tribunal. I suggest to him that if he reads carefully clause 23 of the bill, he will see that it is only in certain cases that the assent of the presiding officer is necessary and, furthermore, that the criticism which he levelled at the president of the tribunal is not wholly justified, because it is stated in the next section to that to which he referred, that_ a majority of the tribunal shall determine its decisions.
But if there are some features of this bill which are not attractive to me, I feel impelled to support it for several reasons. In the first place, it embodies the result of an investigation by men who were eminently qualified to undertake it. True, it is an experiment; true, it invades or seems to invade private property and makes one wonder whether this is not the introduction of a system of state control which, if carried to extremes, might arouse severe controversy throughout the country. But it is a studied and serious attempt to meet the situation; it is an attempt by a government which is confronted by a multitude of problems, to meet the most serious of our financial difficulties. These are times when I believe a government should be upheld, steadied and supported, almost at any cost. I cannot foretell that the administration of this act will be unfair. Furthermore, this measure is put forward as a temporary means of meeting an emergency, and as such I shall support it, not gleefully, not cheerfully, not even hopefully, but under the dictates of duty, praying that it may do something to arrest the growth of debt resulting from the public ownership of our railways, and something to cure this running sore which has sapped our national life for the last ten years.

Mr. Speaker, there are a few observations I desire to make upon the second reading of this bill. I wish, however, to approach the question from a somewhat different angle than that from which it has been approached this afternoon. I have no desire whatever to go into the relative merits of public or private ownership. We find in those countries where the railways are entirely under private ownership they are in exactly the same, if not in a worse position than are our own. I have only to cite the condition of the railways in the United States and Great Britain to show that

my statement in regard to public ownership is correct.
I am in agreement with what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) who has preceded me has said in regard to the canals of this country. According to a report recently submitted to the house, if we allow a certain amount for interest on capital expenditure on our canal systems, it will be found that the annual interest charges will amount to somewhere in the neighbourhood of $14,000,000, while the return for that expenditure is extremely limited.
The previous speaker has made a sort of veiled attack upon the situation of the men employed on our railways. The condition of most of those employees entitles them to a good deal of our sympathy and consideration. When it is realized that on the railroads of this country including the railway shops only from ten to sixteen days per month is being worked, and that the average wage of all men employed on our railroads from the top right down to the bottom is from 55 to 60 cents per hour, the hon. gentleman who preceded me will get some idea of the conditions at the present time amongst the men employed on the railway systems of this country.
With what the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) said in the house this afternoon I am happy to find myself largely in accord. I wish I could say the same regarding the address of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion). I listened very attentively and with appreciation to the very able presentation he made of his case and to his very frank statement. There are just one or two observations I wish to make with reference to some of his statements, and first of all with regard to the character of the men who were appointed to the Duff commission to investigate the railway situation in this country.
The commission was composed of seven gentlemen, no doubt all very estimable in their own way. I find amongst them a lawyer, a doctor, a professor, a bank president, a financier, a gentleman from the United States and a gentleman from Great Britain. The Minister of Railways very frankly stated this afternoon that the appointments from Great Britain and the United States to that commission were made for the purpose of giving protection or representation to the investors in bonds and railway security holders residing in Great Britain and in the United States. Well, Mr. Speaker, if we are going to solve our problems in this country, as naturally I want to see them solved, I believe that we have suffi-

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Heaps
cient intelligence within our own dominion to solve our problems without importing people from outside. In that respect I happen to be a very high protectionist; I believe in a Canada first policy.
But we have in this country a very large element which is also deeply interested in the railway problem. I refer to that vast element which is commonly called the labouring element, the men who work on our railways to the number of 175,000, and many others outside the direct employment of the railways, who received absolutely no representation on this commission. I feel that if the investors in the United States and Great Britain were entitled to representation on the commission because of the money interest, the human element, our own Canadian people, were just as much entitled to representation as were investors in railway securities in other parts of the world. I remember meeting one of the commissioners for the first time in my life after the report had been made, and discussing It with him. I put this question to him. In the first place, Mr. Speaker, I claim that the present situation in which our railways find themselves is due not directly to the policies of the government, present or past, but rather to the economic conditions prevailing throughout this country, and we are now proposing to pass emergency legislation in order to create a prosperous railway situation in this dominion amidst the present dis-53719-177
tressful economic conditions. , Personally I do not think it is possible even with the economies that may be effected under this bill, to bring about a condition of affairs where the two great railways in Canada will be placed in what might be termed a prosperous condition.
The Minister of Railways claimed that the railway problem was the most important problem that we have to face at this particular time. I do not agree. I think that the greatest problem in this dominion that we have got to face at this time is the unemployment problem that is now before parliament. Both problems are connected.

I am quite ready to admit
that there is a connection between the two, but if we are going to solve, or partially solve, the railway problem by intensifying the unemployment problem, our national problems would still be in relatively the same position as at present. Until we get down to a more fundamental basis and deal with the whole of our national life and solve our unemployment problem before we attempt to solve the railway problem, I can see no hope of our solving the railway problem. If the government is going to legislate in the interests of the railways to help them solve their problems, I have a right to ask the government that they should help to solve other national problems, and the first problem to which I would direct their attention is the unemployment problem.
Secondly, I would suggest that they do something to solve the farm problem, which is an extremely serious one in this country. If the basis

of cooperation suggested under this legislation is carried out by the railways of Canada, it is bound to mean abandoned rails and bridges, and a certain amount of abandoned equipment, but on all that abandoned equipment we shall have to continue to pay interest charges even though it may never be used again. On the other hand, 1 would point out that it will involve putting out on the streets, and adding to the number of those already unemployed, men who have worked on our railways during the best years of their lives, which they have given to building up the railways of this country. This is a sound policy of Canada first.

A few weeks ago the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, speaking in the city of Winnipeg, made the following reference to those whom he represented. This was his statement, as it appears in a little pamphlet which I presume most hon. members have received and read:
We cannot agree to turning over to an arbitrary body the conduct of our enterprise and the shaping of our policies, when, in the nature of things, the consequences must be borne by the shareholders. The views of those charged with the responsibility of protecting the enormous investment in the Canadian Pacific would not, in these circumstances, prevail. It has been stated in another place that the first three lines of the bill reading, " An act respecting the Canadian National Railways and to provide for cooperation with the Canadian Pacific railway system, and for other
/796
CAT.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr Gray

purposes," constitute the preamble of the bill, and that having adopted the preamble it means that we have stated openly and publicly that we are against amalgamation of the two systems, or to put it another way, against unified management. I submit, Mr. Speaker, and I shall attempt to show to this house, that the separate identity of these two roads is one in name only.
I have said that anyone giving consideration to the railway situation must be impressed with the need for economies. But are these economies to be effected not only at the expense of the roads but with a total disregard of the humane interests in the roads and in the public service of this country? For several months now we have been deluged with propaganda emanating from the Canadian Pacific Railway, from the president of the road down, pressing upon the Canadian people the thought of amalgamation. I say in all sincerity that I believe the Canadian people would have been much better satisfied had the speech which the Minister of Railways made this afternoon, in which he commended the work of that railway system, been made a few months ago. It is unfortunate that the minister reserved this speech until the bill is about to be enacted into law. The statements he made to-day would have had a settling effect upon the minds of the committee and the people of Canada generally, had they been made a few months ago.
The condition in which we find ourselves with respect to railway financing, and transportation finances generally, is not a new one. At the very outset of the regime of my respected leader (Mr. Mackenzie King) when he took office in 1922 following the general election of 1921, he found a somewhat similar situation. In the very first speech from the throne of his term of office, in the session of 1922, we find these words:
The transportation system -weighs heavily upon our national finances.
And it does to-day. Then he went on to say:
But public ownership will be given a fair trial.
Is there anyone here to-night who will deny that public ownership was given a fair trial from 1921 to 1930 during the years of the King administration.
It was not.

Is there anyone who will deny that during that period there was built up in this country a marvellous railway system of which the Canadian people may justly be proud? During that period large capital ex-

penditures were made. The preservation of the identity of the system has been pledged not only by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) but by the leader of the opposition.

Keep politics out of
it.

When I hear hon. members
opposite say we must keep politics out of the discussion, I am reminded that since we last met in this house hon. members opposite have gone up and down this country hurling a tirade of abuse at the administration of the Canadian National Railways. I shall present for their edification, if for that of no one else, some of the statements of hon. members opposite who, under normal conditions, took a saner view of the situation. In that connection I shall refer to a speech made by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) in the budget debate of 1929. At page 743 of Hansard of that year he is reported as follows:
In respect, however, to the national railway we on this side of the house are all optimists. We look upon that railway as practically our own infant and our own creature.
Then at page 745 we find the following:
Now, when this wonderful Canadian National railway system has more than justified itself, now, that it is rapidly becoming in the nature of a great national asset, now that we may look forward to a day, not perhaps in my lifetime, but in the lifetime of some here, when this system will start repaying the government of Canada part at least of the money it owes to the treasury, to the day when it will have a clean sheet, as it ultimately will have, in regard to its bonded indebtedness to the public; now that the system is in this, a thoroughly prosperous condition, this government desires to treat it as its own creature.
When the Minister of Justice referred to "this government" he referred to the government of my right hon. leader. The minister continues:
Whereas in 1919 it tried to cast it out as base-born now it wants to consider it as its legitimate offspring, and to profit by its success. Let me say, in concluding my remarks on this phase of the subject, that the national railway system in this country constitutes a lasting monument-
I know hon. gentlemen opposite will applaud this statement.
-a lasting monument to the ability and statesmanship and determination of a single man, a member of a former Conservative government, and subsequently Prime Minister of that government. It is to his ability and foresight, to his statesmanship and determination that the people of Canada are indebted for this wonderful system of national railways.

He was
chief pallbearer.

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr Gray

The same right hon. gentleman to whom the minister referred, the leader of the government in another place, takes the child now full grown and leads it gently to a courtship with another, while this government looks about it for the dictator who will tie the knot.
As has been said, the bill is divided into three parts. Part 1 deals with the reorganization of the national railways, part II with authorization of and direction for cooperation; and part III provides for the tribunal which is to be set up to compel cooperation. I agree with the hon. member for York-Sum-bury that it is hard 'to reconcile the terms "compulsory" and "cooperation." Much has been said about part III of the bill. In the debate which took place in another place I believe the main opposition was directed against that part. Here again I may differ from some of my colleagues when I venture the opinion that parts I and II, and not part III, constitute the dangerous elements in the bill.
In effect, part I makes five changes. First, there is provision for the reduction in the board of directors from seventeen to three. Here again I shall follow the hon. member for York-Sunbury when I state that in my view the directorate should not consist of three but of five full time men, one of whom should represent labour. The second provision is for a continuous audit by independent auditors; third, that the president of the road shall no longer be chairman of the board of directors; fourth, that the bond issue, which has been mentioned, will now be made direct by parliament instead of by the railways themselves, and guaranteed by parliament. The fifth provision is for the absolute dissociation of the government from any control whatsoever over the road.
As to the general principles in Nos. 1, 2, 3 and 4 I have no complaint. As has been mentioned to-night, all these matters were discussed by the special committee on railways and shipping, and while not all of the conditions 1 have outlined were brought in as recommendations of that committee, some at least were brought in and the others were approved in committee. We did not need an expensive commission to bring in these recommendations; that could have been done simply iby amending the Canadian National Railways Act. I believe the hon. member for York-Sunbury has said that there is no mention whatever of the work of the committee. I find, however, that that is not the case. The criticism is made that the special committee on railways and shipping is not a necessity and should not again be set up.
I shall deal now with the provision that the board of directors be reduced from seventeen to three. I have said that in my view it should be reduced to only five, but I shall be content to discuss the bill as it appears before me. Only the chairman is full time and in him, as has been stated, is vested virtually the power of a dictator. Why do I say that? Because under section 11 (2) of the bill we find that:
The trustees may decide or act at meetings only by unanimous vote or by majority which includes the chairman.
We have heard this afternoon some suggestions as to what a chairman should be. There are those who say: We must trust the chairman; we must feel and know that he will have the interests of the road and of the country at heart; therefore we should not take any other stand with respect to that matter. We are now discussing not a recommendation of the commission, but the adoption of the cold legal phraseology of this bill. It is not what we may think should happen, it is what is permitted under this bill that I propose to discuss. Others will say: But surely the Minister of Railways or his successor will have something to say with respect to the administration? I say not. This is a government road, the people of Canada are the shareholders, and a cabinet has been elected to represent the shareholders. Under the act as far as I can see the Minister of Railways is mentioned only onice. Section 15 states that the annual reports of the trustees and the auditors respectively shall be submitted to parliament through the Minister of Railways. He becomes a mere messenger of the Canadian National board of trustees, to place upon the table of this house the annual report of these trustees and of the auditors for the time being. From the point of view of economy that may be all right; we can close the minister's office to-morrow when this bill is enacted and save the people $15,000 a year. That may be economy, but it is not responsible government. I will refer to that again.
But before leaving this part let me refer to the manner in which the government proposes to fill vacancies created in this office. The first three directors are appointed by order in council. Any vacancies that may occur are to be filled from a panel of eight, and those picking the panel consist of the president of the exchequer court, the chief commissioner of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and the remaining trustee. I hope I may be pardoned when I say that in my opinion this government, having created this board, are
C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr Gray

seeking to perpetuate their nominees thereon. Why do I say that? I say it because, as I have shown, two of the trustees appointed for seven years form part of this selecting committee, and the chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, an appointee of this government, is one; and I say that this government, knowing that it is going to be in office for only a year, or a short time at best, seeks to perpetuate their appointees upon the people of Canada.
Having set up this machinery, what is proposed by part II of the bill? Let us look at section 16 and see what is possible under it. The hon. member for York-Sunbury and others have said: "No amalgamation." But what I want to point out is that under the powers given to this board, perhaps not amalgamation in the sense of one line being taken over holus-bolus by the other, but under that section piecemeal, this can be accomplished. Section 16 of part II says that the national company-defining it-and the Pacific company-
-are, for the purposes of effecting economies and providing for more remunerative operation, directed to attempt forthwith to agree and continuously to endeavour to agree, and they respectively are, for and on behalf as aforesaid, authorized to agree, upon such cooperative measures, plans and arrangements as are fair and reasonable and best adapted (w-ith due regard to equitable distribution of burden and advantage as between them) to effect such purposes.
That is a general clause. Then subsection 2 says:
Without restricting the generality of the foregoing, any such measures, plans or arrangements may include and be effected by means of-
(a) new companies controlled by stock ownership. . . .
I submit that under that clause if the board of trustees deemed it necessary they could set up a holding company absolutely separate and apart from these two separate identities-
That would be betrayal of trust,

Perhaps so. but I am reading the bill as I see it. Subsection 2 says further:
(b)	leases, entrusting agreements, or licences, or agreements for the pooling and division of earnings arising from the joint operation of any part or parts of freight or passenger traffic. . . .
(e) joint trackage, running rights, joint ownership, or joint operating agreements, depending upon the nature of the property or services included in any cooperative plan.
Let me read (c) putting my own interpretation upon the powers given to this trustee
I Mr. Gray.]
board. Not joint, but "amalgamated" trackage, "amalgamated" running rights, "amalgamated" joint ownership, or "amalgamated" operating agreements-
My hon. friend puts in the word "amalgamated." I think he should make it clear that it is not in the act.

I did, I said that is my own interpretation. And then they could at the end of a year bring in an annual report saying that for the purpose of effecting economies we have deemed it advisable to amalgamate this and that.
Then let me point out that under subsection 3-
All or any of such measures, plans and arrangements may. if agreed to by the parties, he made terminable at will, or on or after stated notice, or for a fixed period or periods or any combination thereof. . . .
In other words, if they think it desirable they can do exactly what president Beatty has been urging this country to do, lease to the Canadian Pacific such portions of the road as they deem advisable for a period of ninety-nine years, and the Minister of Railways as I see it cannot do a thing about it. That to my mind is one of the main dangers of this bill.
Let us contrast for a moment the powers given under the Canadian National Railways Act, with respect to the same matters. I will be very brief; I do not even intend to read the section. Under the Canadian National Railways Act of 1927, chapter 172, revised statutes of Canada, 1927, the side note of section 23 is:
Power to abandon line, and dismantle or dispose thereof by consent.
And the section reads:
With the approval of the governor in council, and upon the recommendation of the Board of Railway Commissioners, the company may abandon the operation of any lines or parts of lines.
And section 24:
W7ith the approval of the governor in council, on the recommendation of the Minister of Rail-ways and Canals . . .
Agreements may be entered into. Before I close I intend to submit a point in connection with that.

What about section 6?
Mr. GRAY': I admit that abuses have crept in; they are bound to creep in. But it was not with respect to matters over which we are now giving power to this dictator or this board that the abuses crept in. If we as a people are to have government ownership, then let

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr Gray
the government of the day take responsibility. If the time has come that we must have one man operation or a dictator of this road, then I am going to take the responsibility of saying that as far as I personally am concerned, I am ready to take the Minister of Railways right now instead of some outside man whom we do not know. I refuse to take that leap in the dark and to give to someone outside these powers over which we as members of parliament or the Minister of Railways cannot have control.
These trustees, may I say, can be removed not by the governor in council but under section 7 only for cause. Section 7 says:
No trustee shall be removed from office, nor suffer any reduction in salary, during the term for which he is appointed, unless for assigned cause and on address of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada.
How much control has this parliament or the government of the day over this dictator that you are about to appoint?
Before I turn for a moment to part III I wish to discuss briefly one section in particular, and I know that in doing so I shall be treading on the toes of some hon. gentlemen from the maritime provinces. Nevertheless I think it should be pointed out at this time to the government and to the people that in subsection 2 of section 14 of this bill there is-to my mind at any rate-an absolute political sop to the maritimes. I note that the hon. member for York-Sunbury is all for the bill on the ground of economy; he hails it as a great measure because it will effect large economies in the conduct of the railways. But immediately he turns round and commends the government for having in the bill the following provision:
The trustees shall so direct, provide and procure that all freight destined for export by sea which is consigned within Canada for carriage to national railways either at point of origin or between that and the sea shall, unless it has been by its shippers specifically routed otherwise, be exported through Canadian seaports.
That subsection is placed in the section dealing with the annual report to parliament. It has no relation whatsoever to the preceding part of the section but is put in there in the hope that it will not be noticed and will slip through. Let us see what will be the operation of economies in respect of that section. The distance from Montreal to Halifax-I am using this illustration because the freight rate is exactly the same-is eight hundred miles, whereas the distance from Montreal to Portland is two hundred and ninety-six miles, though as I say the freight rate is exactly the same in both cases. But
unless the shipper, who does not care which route is followed inasmuch as the rates are the same, specifically directs to the contrary, we must under this bill, this economy measure, ship the long haul down to Halifax; and I have been informed by the railways that the operating costs are approximately proportionate to the mileage. When therefore hon. gentlemen are protesting against talking politics I think it behooves them to read subsection 2 of section 14 of the bill.
As regards part III, I have simply this to say. I doubt very much that it will ever come into effect, but if it does then I say that it must give the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) rather a jolt to find that his resolution with respect to the commonwealth federation has now become a government measure in the form of a bill which permits the confiscation of private property. I imagine that this house little thought that such a proposal would be introduced by the Minister of Railways. I have said that it may never operate, but if it does one finds this thought uppermost- we found it before and it is not new-namely, the placing in the hands of one man of -the power of absolute control. Why do I say that? I say that for this reason: Ostensibly there are three, one to be chosen from the Canadian Pacific and another from the Canadian National; but who will give the deciding judgment of the board? Another superman. As someone has said in this house, there is certainly no room for three supermen in this country, and if we are to have an arbitrary board then I submit that we should have a board of railway commissioners, as suggested by my hon. friend from North Waterloo, a board tried in matters pertaining to railways and with precedents to follow; but certainly I am not in favour of placing this matter in the hands of one man.
In conclusion I would ask the house this question: Are the Canadian National Railways protected by this proposed legislation? I think I have shown that while there are advantages they are far outweighed by the disadvantages, especially when we could bring about these advantages that have been mentioned by simply amending the Canadian National Railway Act. In my opinion this bill which is now before us is a far cry from the speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in Winnipeg in 1930. What did the right hon. gentleman say, speaking in Winnipeg at the time he introduced his campaign?
These were his words:
Here this night, speaking as I am to more than a million of my fellow-countrymen, I say to you that no man in this country rejoices

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bowman
more in the strength and progress of the Canadian National enterprise than I-made possible as it was in the first instance by the genins of our own statesmen and by the passing of legislation by our own party. But, more, more, every effort of mine after July 28 will be for one purpose: That purpose is to preserve not only the identity of the Canadian National Railways as a publicly owned competitor of a private enterprise, but to see that it serves even better and more effectively the Canadian people, who are so proud of it.
And more, I say that if you see any attempt on my part at any time to violate that pledge I give you here and now, then ash for my resignation-insist upon it-for I love my country and wh&t it has done, and one of its greatest achievements has been the development of this great national transportation system of which I believe every Canadian is proud.
Amalgamation? Never. Competition? Ever. That is the policy for which I stand.
Will the government through their minister now undertake that when this bill reaches committee of the whole they will incorporate in it not simply a section such as was read this afternoon with respect to amalgamation, but a real section with teeth in it .making certain that that will not be effective? Will they give an assurance that they will not dissociate themselves absolutely from some form of governmental control under this particular measure? If they will do that and accept some measure of responsibility then I am prepared to support them; if not, then with great reluctance I must vote against the second reading of this bill.

I am
sure the hon. member for West Lambtom (Mr. Gray) will pardon me if I do not follow him in the address which he has just delivered. Frankly, I prefer to follow the example set by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) and the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and attempt to discuss the bill before the house in an entirely non-political attitude.
First, may I congratulate the minister on the very able address which he delivered this afternoon, indicating the most careful preparation and consideration to the end that the house might fully view this great problem which faces Canada to-day. May I say to the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Gray) that while I do not believe that this bill is perfect, I still think that if it receives the approval of the house the excerpts which he read from the speech made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) in 1930 will be just as true as they were at that time. If I thought for one moment that this bill had for its object the amalgamation, merger or unification of the Canadian National with the Canadian Pacific, I would at once oppose

it. However, I do not think that this is the intention of the bill. One feels almost like apologizing to the house for speaking upon this bill after hearing the very able addresses which have been delivered and which cover the subject so thoroughly; nevertheless there are one or two features to which I would like to direct the attention of hon. members, more particularly with the intention of explaining my viewpoint with respect to part III which deals with compulsory cooperation. Perhaps I shall be pardoned if I refer briefly to the earlier history of the railroads in this country.
The Duff report has covered quite thoroughly the history of the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific, and hon. members are so familiar with the subject that I hesitate going into details. There seems to be a feeling that the Canadian National Railways is a failure in public ownership. I am no't an apostle of public ownership, but I think hon. members will agree with me when I say that the Canadian National railway system as we have it in Canada cannot be considered as a true test of public ownership.
I hope not.

C.NR.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bowman
place a high value upon competitive railway service and would foe reluctant to dispense with such competition. Moreover a monopoly would be placed in the hands of a very few, a tremendous power which might be unwisely exercised. I am convinced that amalgamation would result in an unwieldy system which could not be efficiently managed. Amalgamation must necessarily be permanent in effect. Mr. Beatty, in his presentation to the Duff commission, pointed out that a long lease would be necessary-almost a lease in perpetuity. It is not necessary to point out to the house the trouble there would be in unscrambling the two systems after their being for years under one control. I believe that amalgamation must necessarily be permanent in effect and does not envision a brighter future with more business and a greater population, and consequently better times for our railroads.
For the reasons I have set out I submit that amalgamation or unification of the systems is not only undesirable but impossible. Mr. Beatty objects to the arbitral tribunal because he claims that it overides the contract his company made with the government at the time of its incorporation, and states further that the company were guaranteed certain privileges and rights which were to continue in effect during their term of incorporation. However while Mr. Beatty objects to restraint upon the operations of the Canadian Pacific Railway he is in favour of restraining the operations of the Canadian National Railways. Throughout his speeches he has complained of extravagance on the part of the government railways as being responsible for large expenditures of his own company.
I say that if the Canadian National system is to be under restraint, and the Canadian Pacific is not, there would be a policy of hands off the C.P.R. and hands on the C.N.R. After all. the board which is to be set up is to settle disputes-that is all, and no more. While in the initial stages I perhaps had some doubts as to whether or not I was in favour of compulsory cooperation, the remarks made by Mr. Beatty before the commission finally determined my attitude. When discussing the proposition before the Duff commission that there be unification of the two systems for purposes of administration Mr. Leman made the following statement:
That is where we want enlightenment.
Mr. Beatty replied:
Well, if you can find a way to eliminate the government in the interim we will be taking a long step in the right direction. I am as
(Mr. Bowman.]
convinced as I am sitting here that if three years from now there was .an upturn in business which was, say, substantial, we would meet the same kind of competition and competitive extravagances that we have faced in the last eight years, and while we think we have learned the lesson and won't be extravagant, I do not believe we will realize that hope.
So Mr. Beatty states that if conditions were to improve, at the end of three years there would be just as many extravagances on the part of the publicly owned system as there have been in the past. Consequently he advocates restraint of some kind upon that system. I say if there is to be restraint upon the government railways there should be a like restraint upon the Canadian Pacific Railway and for the reason he sets out, if for nothing else, I should be in favour of the arbitral boards or tribunals which under the provisions of the bill are to be set up.
I feel that section 23, which refers to the powers of tribunals, will have to be amended in certain respects. The effect of that section as at present drafted goes, I believe, much farther than either the Senate or the government intended it should go. Section 23 is as follows:
Where the execution of an order, or the carrying out of a decision of a tribunal, involves the doing of any act which by any statute requires, but for the provisions of this act, the leave, sanction, assent or approval of the board of railway commissioners, or where in the opinion of the presiding officer the public interests involved are of sufficient importance to warrant it, no order made by a tribunal shall be operative without the concurrence of the presiding officer and his formal written assent.
I should like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that the first part of the paragraph provides that the chairman of the tribunal, who is chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, shall give his assent in respect of measures which are within the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners. With that I agree.

But with respect to the second part ol the paragraph, with regard to all other matters which the chairman believes involve an important public interest, any matter of major importance or one which might be dealt with by five members of the board instead of three, he must in that case, too, give his assent to any order which may be made. Mr. Speaker, rising to speak at this
time may I say that I realize why the hon. member who has preceded me (Mr. Bowman) has so spoken. There are some features of the bill on which I believe the house is absolutely in agreement, one of which is the necessity of cooperation, cooperation that is full and practical. Surely the railroads and the country as a whole must have learned in the school of bitter experience that cooperation is necessary under present conditions. Experience in recent years surely has taught us that lesson for many years to come.
As far as economies are concerned I believe it has been wdlil expressed and emphasized this afternoon and evening that the human factor cannot be forgotten or neglected. Service must also be maintained in some sections of the country. That has always been recognized in the past, and with a new country like Canada even during the present time of stress we must keep up certain capital expenditures and services. And this applies particularly as far as maintenance of service is concerned. As has been so well said by previous speakers, surely the two railways when considering measures of economy cannot any longer place the whole burden upon the working men or the train crews. I share the view expressed a little while ago that of every three dollars the railway companies have saved in recent years two dollars have been saved by curtailing wages and the number of men employed, which is not fair to that class of people. We can go too far in that respect. It is my duty to deal at length with a very important matter, important for my section of the country. The misgiving I feel in that regard is not that I must take the time of the house, but that I may be unable with my limited ability to put as forcibly as I should like the matters relating to our railway systems as they affect our section of the country and the whole of Canada. So I shall concentrate my remarks particularly on that section of the Canadian National railway system which is known as the National Transcontinental.
For the last six years, since I have had the honour of representing the riding of North Timiskaming in this house I have made it my duty to consider this all-important problem and speak of it in this house every year. Outside of our local papers I am sorry to state that so far the result has been disappointing, in that I have never received any support from the press of the large centres of population, never a single line from the daily papers of Toronto or Montreal. The
only support came, I think, from the maritime provinces, the Winnipeg Free Press and some of the western papers. I feel that my arguments are worthy of attention and should receive consideration. Being fully seized of the fairness of my case I am going to avail myself of every opportunity that is afforded me to impress this house and the country with its importance, and I feel confident that I shall receive more support than I have in the past.
I am going to divide my argument into three parts; first, a brief analysis of the Duff report itself, and the personnel of the commission; second the National Transcontinental question; and third, the present proposals. On account of the limited time that a member has at his disposal I am going to deal first with the ail-important question of the National Transcontinental.
When on July 30, 1903, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, launching the project in parliament, introduced the bill for the construction of the National Transcontinental, he used these words:
This new railway will be another link in that chain of union. It will not only open territory hitherto idle and unprofitable; it will not only force Canadian trade into Canadian channels; it will not only promote citizenship between old Canada and new Canada, but it will secure us our commercial independence, and will forever make us free from the bondage of tbe bonding privilege.
These were the statements of a man of vision; indeed they were almost a prophecy. If that great departed statesman could travel in our section of the country to-day he would see that prophecy coming into fulfilment during the present generation. He would see new centres of population, starting from Quebec city to Harvey Junction, and sweeping along the St. Maurice valley, rich in timber and hydro developments, up to the height of land in northern Quebec, which is part of the clay belt abounding in natural resources, and a most promising mining field that will astound the world during the next twenty years; on to northern Ontario with its clay belt and mining and industrial districts where a new town like Kapuskasing has given during normal times in freight and passenger earnings for that section from $150,000 to $300,000 per month. You have in that route the most direct and easiest gradient from the prairies to the St. Lawrence. That section of the line was never intended for local traffic, that was not its purpose. The initial purpose was to give the most direct communication between east and west. When that section was constructed there was practically no population through there, but we have now nearly 200,000 souls. The main reason, in fact the only

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bradette
reason why the connecting link was built out of the public treasury, was to give better communication between east and west. However, Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to make a speech on that subject; my purpose is to have the house and the country realize that if to-day we have a larger deficit than we should on the Canadian National railway system it is partly due to the fact that the original ideas that prompted the construction of that railway have not been carried out. I would not be working so strenuously or speaking so often on this subject if our wheat and our cattle were moving through Canadian channels. I regret to say that nearly forty per cent of our wheat and heavy freight from the west finds its way out through American ports. I maintain that a large proportion of the national railway deficit would be removed if our freight travelled by its proper routing, the line of least resistance. Again I say I do not pretend to make a speech, but. I desire to place before this parliament and the country a brief showing why the national transcontinental was built and asking why it has not been properly used.
I hold in my hand a circular issued I believe, by the port commissioners of Halifax and Saint John, entitled, Is Canada for the Canadians? I am going to read some parts of it so that the house will be seized of the situation as it actually exists:
A Ruinous Drain
The fundamental trade policy of Canada is the east-and-west policy. This policy was embedded in the conception of confederation, and all through the years it has been recognized as the only true Canadian policy.
Many hundreds of millions of dollars of Canadian public money have been spent to perpetuate this policy and to ensure its success. The greatest single effort for the projection of the east-and-west policy was the construction of the transcontinental railway at an ultimate cost to the Canadian people of $330,000,000.

These are astounding figures, showing in what enormous quantities Canada has permitted the diversion of its own traffic from its own channels.
This ruinous drain upon Canada's economic vitality must cease.
It continues in the same vein until we come to the last paragraph:
The chairman of the Halifax harbour commission has stated his belief that the port of

Halifax has just about reached the limit of its development unless an adequate share of the Canadian grain traffic can be secured, for, manifestly, it is going to he difficult, if not impossible, to develop any turn-around movement of liner tonnage under existing conditions.
In these circumstances, so vital not to this port and province alone, but to the dominion, as a national matter, we respectfully urge an early hearing of the appeal in the transcontinental grain rates ease, and a favourable decision in the interests of our own transportation channels.
The maritime provinces have cooperated with us in this all-important matter.
I am going to give hon. members the situation as it actually exists. When the road was completed in 1916 it was able to quote a rate of six cents per bushel on wheat from Armstrong, a station in the Thunder Bay district just north of lake Nipigon and almost due north of Port William and Port Arthur, down to Quebec city, a distance of 959 miles. But then a mysterious thing happened, the reason for which I have never been able to discover-hardly had the rate been announced than the Conservative government almost quadrupled it. If the railroad was making money with a six cent rate, why was that traffic taken away from us? The increased rate proved to be not only discriminatory but almost prohibitive, because I believe that after 1924 not a single bushel of wheat or a single carload of cattle has been routed from Winnipeg over the National Transcontinental. The expected volume of traffic never developed. There is some local traffic, but, as I said before, this section of the road was never intended for local traffic. When the road was built this section of the country was considered to be a wilderness. I can remember when the government of the province of Quebec granted certain timber, mineral and mining rights to a Belgian company, at that time northern Quebec and northern Ontario were considered as being practically wildernesses. We have developed quite a large population and a considerable local traffic, but the original idea in building the National Transcontinental was to take care of through freight and passenger traffic from ocean to ocean.
In 1921 the Quebec harbour commission made representations to the board of railway commissioners in connection with the 20.7 cents per bushel rate then in force on the Arm-strong-Quebec division. A sitting of the board was held in Quebec city with the late Hon. Frank Carvell presiding. We expected that we would receive fair treatment from the railway commissioners, but here is what hap-

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Bradette
pened. An extraordinary argument was used by the chief commissioner that if the rate was reduced, it would mean ruin for other railways. Mr. Carvel! said:
If my conception of the National Transcontinental was right, when it was started and when it was being built, I think freight can be transported over that line at a figure which would mean the absolute ruination of other railways in Canada. If not, we were all wrong and we were not justified in building it.
There was justification in building that section of the road but there is no justification in leaving it idle at the present time. These high rates are hurting the maritimes, northern Quebec and northern Ontario and the whole of Canada. I believe they have an adverse effect upon the western provinces as well. If the western provinces would study this question I believe they would find that the natural routing for their wheat, at least during the winter months, is from Winnipeg to Quebec and down to Halifax and Saint John. At the present time from forty to forty-five per cent of our wheat goes through American seaports. This matter vitally affects the maritime provinces because with the grain being routed as it is at the present time, an unreasonable amount finds an outlet through Buffalo and Montreal to Boston and Portland and other American ports. Were this traffic routed over the transcontinental to Quebec it could be profitably moved after the close of navigation on the St. Lawrence from the ancient capital via the old Intercolonial road to Halifax and Saint John. The present rate on wheat over the 959 miles stretch from Armstrong to Quebec is 20-7 cents per bushel, while the rate from Port Arthur to Edmonton, a distance of 1,305 miles, is only 15-6 cents per bushel. The rate per mile through northern Ontario to Quebec is about double what it is on the prairies. If an eleven cent rate were made effective to Quebec, it would immediately create a maximum rate upon the great lakes. The Canadian Pacific rate from Goderich to Halifax, a distance of 1,305 miles, is 12J cents per bushel, a rate considerably less than that prevailing from prairie points to the head of the lakes. The rate from Fort William to Halifax, a distance of 1,753 miles, is 21-3 cents per bushel while the rate from Armstrong to Quebec, a distance of only 959 miles, is 20-7 cents a bushel. A moment ago I quoted from a circular dealing with this all important question. I was glad to note that at the late imperial conference it was decided that grain being shipped to Great Britain should follow an all Canadian route. I hope that no loopholes will be found in this regulation because this route is the logical
route for grain shipments, especially during the winter months.
Grain is not the only thing which this transcontinental road can deliver most expeditiously. On a trial shipment of 600 steers, the running time of the train between Winnipeg and Quebec was eighteen hours less than it would have been from Winnipeg to Montreal. Two feedings only were sufficient whereas three are normally required. This fact, coupled with the lessened shrinkage in the shipment, represented a saving of not less than $5 per head, or, roughly, S3,000 upon the whole consignment. This experiment was carried on for one winter only and I cannot understand why it was not continued. Is it because we have not sufficient population in these sections to command a certain number of votes? I believe the only way that this situation can be remedied is by bringing forward the facts as forcibly as possible. If it was a parochial or local matter I would not bring it to the attention of the house, but I believe it is more than that. If hon. members from the maritimes, the province of Quebec, the province of Ontario and the three western provinces would study this situation I believe they would find a reduced rate would be beneficial to the country as a whole.
We are in the pioneering sections of Canada and I cannot understand why the older sections of the country do not realize the true position. At times we contend, and perhaps rightly so, that the larger centres of population in Ontario and Quebec are against us. If the traffic which goes from the head of the lakes through American ports was kept in Canada, there would not be so much criticism, but this is not the case, as I have shown, a large percentage of it is entirely lost to Canadian traffic. In 1921 Commissioner Rutherford made a statement in response to a request for lower rates, so when I have another occasion to speak on some of the features of this bill I am going to refer to what a former commissioner had to say as to what happened in our section of the country. This is Commissioner Rutherford's statement:
This is something that has to be general in a very careful way. When we consider the . elevator system at Fort William and Port Arthur, the tremendous machinery created for the movement of that grain crop, to introduce a revolutionary method like the making of a special rate on any one road would mean disturbing the whole movement of grain, such a disturbance as would bring about economic disaster for the time being.
We do not want any special favours or any special rate in our section of the country; we desire only equalization of rates, the same

rate as exists in other sections. When we apply to the Board of Railway Commissioners, we do not go there as mendicants; we want to receive the same attention as the rest of Canada is getting, and fair play, that is all. The commission did not make any difficulty about giving its reasons why the rates should be made high: If the road carried grain as cheaply as it could, in view of its superior construction and low grades, other roads, less favourably circumstanced, could not compete, and therefore it must not be allowed to make low rates. This is certainly not a statement from a national point of view, not a statement worthy of a commissioner. Every section of the country should receive the same treatment. I do not like to make this observation, but in our section of the country we feel that because of our small population we are not receiving the treatment to which we are entitled. But without trying to prophesy, I believe, that within the next twenty years instead of 200,000 we shall have a population of at least half a million, and then perhaps we shall be treated more favourably than we are at the present time. I have, however, enough confidence in the fair-mindedness and justice of the present Minister of Railways to believe that, although the particular locality in which he resides may be adversely affected, he will use his influence to see to it that the Canadian National system in our section receives from the railway commission the just treatment it deserves.
A ruling has been made in regard to reading certain extracts. I believe that I shall be in order now in reading a memorial presented by the Cochrane board of trade and, I believe, distributed to all members of parliament ten or twelve months ago. It deals with the matter in a very thorough manner and I am going to read it to the house. It states:
The National Transcontinental railway from Quebec to Winnipeg was conceived and built for the most direct and economical transportation of passengers and freight between eastern and western Canada, and for this purpose it was constructed with a minimum of grades and curves. In the early years of its operation, it was shown that grain could be hauled from western Canada to eastern seaports in greater quantities and at a cheaper rate per train than over any other Canadian railway.
But since this demonstration, it appears that the National Transcontinental railway has been discriminated against by the increase in the freight rate on wheat to help its competitor thereby defeating the very purpose for which it was built and diverting much of our wheat haulage to American territory and to American ships.
fMr. Bradette.]
I believe, in thus mentioning the anomaly, it is stating the case properly.
The possibilities of this railway do not seem to be known and appreciated as they should be by the people of Canada, by the members of parliament or even by the administrative heads of our railway systems.
No doubt this was an allusion to the railway commissioners, because after a great deal of expenditure and much travelling, we could not get a proper judgment from that commission.
Recently the Canadian National trains 1 and 2 between Montreal and Vancouver, which have been running through Cochrane for fifteen years, have been rerouted via Capreol, thereby missing 400 miles of what is perhaps the most prosperous mining, timber, agricultural and tourist district in Canada, namely: between North Bay and Hearst.
Therefore, the Cochrane Board of Trade humbly requests the royal commission and the president of the Canadian National Railways to consider its claims for a restoration of proper passenger and freight service between Winnipeg, Quebec, Halifax, Montreal and Toronto by Cochrane over the National Transcontinental railway of the Canadian National lines for the following amongst other reasons:
(A) Re: Passenger Service
1.	A glance at a map of Canada shows the National Transcontinental line as the most direct link between Quebec and Winnipeg.
2.	This line was constructed with a minimum of grades and curves, permitting fast travel and heavy haulage.
3.	It passes through the prosperous agricultural, mining, timber and tourist districts of Northern Quebec and Northern Ontario.
4.	It is linked at Herve junction with Montreal; at Taschereau with Rouyn and Kirkland Lake; at Cochrane with Montreal, Toronto, Cobalt silver camp, Kirkland Lake and Timmins gold camps, the lower and upper clay belts of Northern Ontario, and the James Bay basin; at Hearst with the Algoma Central railway from Sault Ste. Marie; at Nakina, with Sudbury and Port Arthur districts, at Sioux Lookout with Fort William districts.
5.	The possibilities of increase in population and thus in passenger traffic are greater in the territory traversed by it, than along any other transcontinental line in Ontario and Quebec, owing to the agricultural, mining and timber resources that it taps.
6.	There are greater attractions and interest for cross-country passengers in the territory served by the National Transcontinental railway than along the other railroads.
7.	The mining camps of Tashota. Red Lake, Manitoba and the Peace River were mostly opened up and developed by prospectors and' mining men from the Cobalt, Kirkland Lake and Porcupine camps of Northern Ontario and the National Transcontinental railway is the logical means of communication between them.
