which crosses the only territory in Northern Ontario capable of greater agricultural, mining and industrial development.
9.	Although there is duplication between the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian National railway in other parts of Ontario and Quebec, there is no duplication of the Quebec to Winnipeg railway line.
10.	A fast, complete and economical passenger service between Winnipeg and Toronto, Montreal, Quebec and Halifax could be maintained by routing the Toronto-Vancouver trains over the old Grand Trunk railway via North Bay, joining there with the Montreal trains, and proceeding over the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway to Cochrane where connections with the Quebec trains can also be made.
11.	Towns were built up along the National Transcontinental railway and industries developed with the expectation of continued main line traffic and at present passenger service is practically cancelled from Hearst westwards to Nakina along this line.
(B) Re: Freight Service
1.	The straight line between Quebec and Winnipeg, with an excellent road-bed and minimum of curves and grades favours rapid and economical haulage of heavy freight trains.
2.	The junctions at Sioux Lookout, Nakina, Hearst, Cochrane, Taschereau, and Herve also support the contention that the National Transcontinental railway should be put to greater use in cross country freight haulage.
3.	During the war, a huge quantity of freight was hauled over this line at a lower tonnage cost thau any other transcontinental railroad.
4.	The winter haulage of grain to Canadian Atlantic seaports can be accomplished more economically over this road.
5.	The rapidity of development of Northern Quebec and of Northern Ontario is an assurance of increasing incoming and outgoing freight.
6.	By using the old Grand Trunk line between Toronto and North Bay, and the Ontario government owned Temiskaming and Northern Ontario railway between North Bay and Cochrane, the National Transcontinental railway can handle the Toronto-Winnipeg freight to greater advantage.
7.	The diversion of Canadian grain to American ships, railroads and elevators with resulting loss of wages to Canadian workmen should be prevented and the National Transcontinental railway restored to its proper object of hauling western grain to Canadian Atlantic seaports and carrying eastern products and imports westwards.
S. Of the three transcontinental lines crossing Ontario; Canadian Pacific, Canadian Northern and National Transcontinental, the last is the more suitable for rapid and economical haulage and crosses the most populated, prosperous and promising agricultural, mining and timber districts, suitable for the establishment of one million more Canadian citizens.
I believe I have built up a case for the National Transcontinental, and it is up to parliament in this new legislation to ensure that our section of the country receives the treatment it deserves. Why should the people
of Canada spend 8170,000,000 for the mere pleasure of building a road, through what was then a wilderness, over which freight could be forbidden to flow? Certainly that was not the intention of those who constructed the transcontinental system.
As I stated at the outset, it was never the intention .to build that section of road purely for local traffic. It is true that up to three or four years ago, only with local traffic, that section of the road was self-supporting, and I believe it is self-supporting at the present time, but it was not intended for local traffic alone. We never, however, received the quota of through traffic we were entitled to get. This applies more particularly to grain and also to cattle. It may surprise hon. members to hear that, although we have the most direct route, for instance from Halifax to Winnipeg and Vancouver, we have never had a single sack of European mail going over our section of the road. It was always moved the other way. It may surprise hon. members also to hear that if I buy a carload of feed or flour to be delivered in the town of Cochrane from Winnipeg, instead of coming in the most direct way from Winnipeg to Cochrane, that carload is billed to Fort William or Port Arthur, from there routed over the Canadian Pacific up to North Bay, and then from North Bay to Cochrane, providing almost double the amount of traffic it should.
I have spoken on this subject on several occasions, Mr. Speaker, and no matter how much the members of this parliament may resent the fact of my speaking about it so often, I intend to bring it up as of-ten as possible until I get the ear of parliament and of the press, and the country realizes the anomaly in the present situation. We maintain that if we had the traffic to which we are entitled the Canadian nation would not lose any traffic, and that is without prejudice to the Canadian Pacific. It would simply be throwing into Canadian channels the traffic that is passing through foreign channels. I believe in the policy of Canada first to the greatest possible extent.

I pass now to the subject which brought me to my feet, and that is part I and part I only, of the bill, which relates entirely to the management of the Canadian National Railways. As you will remember, Mr. Speaker, it was brought out by previous speakers and by the minister when he moved the second reading this afternoon, that part I provides for three trustees to administer the affairs of the Canadian National Railways, a chairman and two others. The chairman under the bill has the power of veto. He can initiate nothing without a majority vote, but he can veto anything.
It was further stated that the three trustees must be so located that they would be available immediately for consultation, the chairman being a full time man and the other two trustees being immediately available whenever required. I think that that must mean, Mr. Speaker, that all three trustees must live in the immediate vicinity of Montreal. The two who are to be part time men must almost be residents of the district in the immediate vicinity of Montreal.
They should all be full time.

Certainly they should all be full time, and they should not all come from the immediate vicinity of Montreal. I listened to the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) this afternoon when he objected to any trustee being chosen for geographical reasons. With all due deference I am going to advance a contrary argument. I ask the house to remember that in this bill we are dealing with two railway systems but with two systems which are essentially different in structure. One, the Canadian Pacific, was built deliberately and purposely as a system. If mistakes were made they were errors of judgment; but it was built, as one might say, from the inside out. The other, sir, was simply an aggregation of bankrupt railways which were picked up, placed under a common management and an effort made to consolidate them into a system. It was not built scientifically. With all due deference I submit that it cannot ever be managed on a hardheaded business basis, as could the other corporation, without grave danger to the structure of the country. I know that that is an unpopular statement to make, but let me elaborate.
We have within the system a large number of branch lines, part of the old Transcontinental lines, and the old Intercolonial railway. Some of them have never paid and may never pay-although perhaps that is too broad a statement. Let me, however, take the Intercolonial as a starting point. I wish to give one or two illustrations. The Intercolonial-and this time I believe the hon. member for West Lambton will find corroboration for my statement an the British North America Act, section 133-the Intercolonial was, one may say, the quid pro quo for the entrance of the maritime provinces into confederation.
How many quid pro quos did you get?

I do not know, but certainly we deserved more than we ever got. The Intercolonial was the quid pro quo, because through it our products were to flow to central Canada, and the products of central Canada were to flow to us, our ports being used for export to the markets of the world. We have surrendered a good deal, so far as the Intercolonial railway is concerned. We surrendered what I believe to be part of our constitutional rights when the Intercolonial became part of the Canadian National railway system. I did not disapprove of the change, but I say that the railway was not built as a commercial enterprise; it was built primarily as a military enterprise, and followed almost the longest possible route in an effort as far as possible to get away from the United States border. I am fearful that if such a railway is placed under the control of a purely business admini-

C.N.R.-C.P.R. Bill-Mr. Ernst
stration, which will not have at heart the history of Canada, damage may be done to the structure of confederation. As a member from the maritime provinces I should like to be sure that those provinces will have representation on the board of trustees in order that the integrity of the old Intercolonial may in some measure be preserved. I do not ask for control-although judging from what we have given to the rest of Canada we might also ask for that-but I do ask that we have some representative whose voice may be heard urging our problems, when they arise, before a decision is given.
I am fearful that on a basis of pure dollars and cents irreparable injury may be done. I ask the hon. member for Vancouver Centre whether he has not the same fears for the Pacific slope, although he has not the bond of the British North America Act to help him out. I am in sympathy with him.
Let me give another illustration. I shall take a branch line such as that running through my constituency. This branch line is supposed to be losing money. Under a board of three trustees from one centre, what will happen? They are charged with making the railway pay, if it is humanly possible, and I have no doubt they will try to do their duty. If they do, what happens? They will look at a report from this branch line and take note that traffic on this particular line is light. They will decide that they can handle the traffic with less trains per week than are now running. Possibly where there are twelve trains per week they would attempt to give the service with six or seven. The interests of the trustees would be purely financial, those of the Canadian National railways and nothing else. They know nothing about the national considerations or the vision which prompted the building of many of these lines. They know that dividends have to be paid in dollars and cents, and for that reason they will say: "We will handle that traffic with so many trains a week."
Quite right.
What happens? I will give the hon. member an illustration, because obviously he lives on the main line.
No, I do not.

I shall give an illustration.
We will take a fish firm which caters to the fresh fish trade of Canada, and employs between three and four hundred men. In order to continue business that firm must be able to make express shipments instantly. Restrict train service, and that firm might

become bankrupt and the men would have to walk out on the street. Nothing else could happen. What is true of that firm is true of many others. I have no doubt the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth knows of many more firms in his constituency which would be in the some position. If we run the branch lines on a pure dollars and cents basis without taking into consideration the national interest, we will put a good many men on the street who are now earning decent livings.
As I have said, the Canadian National railways were not built as a railway system, but were built by those who had vision and who had faith in the future of the country. Let me give one further illustration in connection with the same branch line. Obviously if those who sit at the head, with the blue pencil, are interested only in the production of dividends, those who manage the affairs on the main line will try to make a good showing, even at the expense of the branch lines. The whole Atlantic region is under one management. What has been happening? Branch lines are saddled with every possible expense which can be piled on to them, so that the burdens of the main lines may be lightened. In December three locomotives were sent from the main lines to this particular branch line. W7hen they got down there they wheezed, whistled and died and had to be sent back to the main line for repairs. Those repairs were charged to the branch line. The main line saved the expense. Its shops were credited with the repairs. If that happens now, what will happen if there is nobody on the board of trustees who has knowledge of local conditions? I put that question to hon. members, and speak feelingly, because after the damage has been done it will be too late.
I now come to the point I have been trying to illustrate, namely that the board of trustees should consist of five members, and I am prepared to support an amendment to that effect. I believe that all five members should be full time members-all of them. I believe the west should have representation, not in order that there might be political or geographical pull, but in order that these peculiar conditions of which I speak might be brought to the notice of the board before it took responsibility for making a decision. I am afraid of the decision that will be made by men sitting in Montreal who perhaps do not know a single thing about the region concerning which they are making the decision.
About the branch lines.

No, more than the branch
lines. I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that if the

legislation goes through as the bill now stands many members will come back here at the next session regretting having so voted.
There are other features of the bill of which I do not entirely approve, but which I am prepared to support. I realize the need for every possible economy consistent with the national interest. But my point is that I believe there is an interest greater than the interest of the dollar, and that is the interest of the Canadian people as a whole. I welcome the announcement of the Minister of Railways this afternoon that minor amendments will be considered on their merits, and that the government is willing to accept them if they are in the interests of Canada. I implore the government either to move or to accept an amendment making the board of trustees five and assuring the country that every part will have representation thereon.
I do not speak as a defeatist with relation to the Canadian National. I realize that the problem is acute, but after all it is not much more acute than the problem every one of us has to face to-day. I am confident that we have turned the corner; we are facing prosperity, all we have to do is to go towards it. I speak only as a private member; my opinion may be worth nothing, and I hope it gives offence to none, but I regard the collapse of the financial structure of the great republic to the south of us as the first herald of the dawn. I cannot help but regard it so; for I have always thought, and have stated publicly-not because I have any dislike for the United States; I have two brothers earning their living there-my earnest conviction that the United States has been chiefly responsible for the world collapse. I have always predicted that before we can recover they would have to go through torture and pain. I hope the pain will become no greater, but I am satisfied that from what has happened will result the turn towards a stable international monetary basis, which is the first prerequisite for recovery. When we do that I am satisfied it is going to be on the basis of inflation in the United States; that our dollar, being shackled to the American dollar, will be inflated; that commodity prices will rise, the revenues of the railways will increase, our governmental revenues will go up, our private revenues will go up, and our troubles will be over.
